subtopic: NORTH VIET NAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he has anything to report to the house on whether the international control commission carried out investigations into the shipment of men and materials into North Viet Nam by the communists. Also, would he care to make any observations on statements by Hugh Campbell, a retired R.C.A.F. adviser of the Canadian delegation, to the effect that the Canadian members of the Viet Nam truce team should long ago have expressed their complaints about the presence of P.T. boats? Mr. Campbell said P.T. boats were outlawed by the Geneva agreement of 1954 under which the three man Polish, Indian and Canadian teams were established. Among other things Mr. Campbell said Canadians always backed down when Polish members of the inspection team called the vessels fishing boats.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Secrelary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NORTH VIET NAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the international control commission in Viet Nam is, of course, made up of three countries. The limitations attending the operations of the commission arise largely from the insistence by at least one member that no action can be taken without unanimity on the part of all three members. This has hampered somewhat, as the right hon. gentleman will realize, not only in the immediate past but earlier, even during the days when his government was faced with this situation, the operations of the commission. Nevertheless the commission continues, particularly in circumstances such as these, to serve a useful purpose. There are now five teams of the commission in North Viet Nam. We are hoping to receive a report based on their observations. That report has not of course come in as yet, but I hope that later we will be in a position, assuming there
is general agreement among the members of the commission, to say something further.

subtopic: NORTH VIET NAM
speechtext: What about the question I asked relative to the criticism of the air force officer who was an attache, to the effect that Canadians always back down, and the Polish statement that these P.T. boats which are being concentrated are simply fishing boats? Will the secretary of state also tell us what information he has regarding the alleged considerable addition of aircraft contributed by red China within the last 24 hours?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NORTH VIET NAM
speechtext:
With regard to the arrival of Chinese aircraft in the last 24 hours I cannot offer any information except to pass on to the right hon. gentleman and to the house what has already apparently been said publicly by the United States secretary of defence, who said it was possible Chinese aircraft would be given to North Viet Nam.
With regard to charges about Canadian participation in the commission, I think the right hon. gentleman, who has had some experience as head of the government, will agree with me, that the Canadian member of the commission-and I have investigated this-during the period of ten years has given a lead and has taken the position, particularly since 1962 when the right hon. gentleman was in office, that in the absence of the unanimity rule the commission should be able to act on the basis of a decision by two members.
If the commission has not been able to fully discharge its responsibilities, I am satisfied after a careful examination of the evidence, that the fault does not rest with Canada. I would hope particularly in the present situation, when the commission may render useful service, both the Polish and Indian members will accede to the position of Canada, that the commission's good offices should be used where asked.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Will he comment on the report made by a United Nations spokesman that the fighting in Cyprus that occurred yesterday is the heaviest yet, and in general and perhaps specifically will he tell us whether a note has been received by the United Nations signed by President Makarios indicating that the United Nations forces on Cyprus should have access to all areas of the island?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FREEDOM OF MOVEMENT OF UN FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian high commissioner has reported today that Turkish Cypriots began to build fortifications on the green line on the morning of August 5. Despite assertions to the contrary they improved their positions later in the day when United Nations troops withdrew because they screened the line of fire.
The secretary general has received a further communication from the head of the government of Cyprus assuring the United Nations forces freedom of movement on the island, a position different from the one he took ten days ago.

speechtext: supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. May I ask the minister whether he has received a copy of this further letter from Archbishop Makarios; and will it be tabled? subtopic: STUDENT LOANS-INQUIRY AS TO APPLICATION PROCEDURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance, the urgency of which deserves his immediate attention. I have received some complaints from university students who are not able to avail themselves of the student loans because it seems the proper machinery is not set up as yet.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STUDENT LOANS-INQUIRY AS TO APPLICATION PROCEDURE
speechtext:
We had a fairly extensive debate on the student loans bill, Mr. Speaker, and as I remember it was explained that the machinery for making loans would be worked out with the provinces and that it would take some time. In fact, if I remember correctly, I said it would take at least a month to work out the machinery. This was one of the reasons some hon. members thought it was important to get the bill through as quickly as possible. We are in touch with the provinces and the banking institutions, and I have received a number of letters on the same subject. I think it is important to advise students or applicants that it will be the end of August or early


September before all the arrangements have been worked out in detail.

subtopic: STUDENT LOANS-INQUIRY AS TO APPLICATION PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question?
Can the Minister of Finance tell us if his department has figured out the amounts of the alternative payments to be made to the province of Quebec and if those calculations were made according to the formula given in Bill No. C-110?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STUDENT LOANS-INQUIRY AS TO APPLICATION PROCEDURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, these arrangements are being negotiated with the government of Quebec which, I think, is perhaps the proper authority to speak for the province on this matter. I have nothing to report in specific terms to the house, at this time. When I have I shall be glad to do so.

subtopic: STUDENT LOANS-INQUIRY AS TO APPLICATION PROCEDURE
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. What arrangements will the minister's department make to publicize the procedures which a student must follow in order to apply for these loans? The minister recognizes there will not be much time, since the machinery will not be ready until the end of August. There will have to be definite procedures outlined so the student will know what to do. What is the minister's intention?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STUDENT LOANS-INQUIRY AS TO APPLICATION PROCEDURE
speechtext: Except in any province that decides to handle the matter on its own, the student will apply to the authority designated by the province. Until the provinces have settled how they want to handle this matter it will be impossible to advise the student in detail what to do. However, we are drafting a booklet or brochure which will contain this information. We will not be able to complete it until the arrangements with the provinces have been completed. In the meantime I think if hon. members who are receiving requests for information would suggest to the students that they apply either to the loan boards that are set up in the provinces, with which they are familiar, or to the university authorities, this would be the best course to take for the time being.

subtopic: STUDENT LOANS-INQUIRY AS TO APPLICATION PROCEDURE
speechtext:
May I put a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker?
Could the Minister of Finance tell us whether any province other than Quebec has expressed its intention of taking advantage of the alternative payments instead of the provisions of the act itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
It
contains no hint whatsoever of government policy on national highway development. We now know that the forest access program has gone. The roads to resources program has gone, and no indication is given here that any agreement has been reached with the provinces to continue a program for the development of roads or highways, except for a new policy which can only be called a squeaking wheel policy; in other words, where the squeal is loudest the grease is applied thickest.
I say this because in the absence of a national policy, despite the necessity of such a policy, we heard from the Minister of Transport with regard to the construction of roads in one particular province. I will quote his words as they appear in Hansard on page 6425:
Of course, we realize that road building comes under the provinces, but we are told that there is such a backlog in Quebec's road building and rebuilding program that the Gaspe highway will not be completed before several years, unless special financial assistance is provided in that connection.
Does not that same condition prevail in all the provinces of Canada? What kind of an excuse for policy is this? If we are to have a national government legislating in the national interest it should surely produce a better reason than that in order to justify an ad hoc arrangement with one province when the other nine provinces all have similar problems of at least equal urgency.
I make no complaint about a contribution to the Quebec road building program providing the government will indicate in its legislative program, or somewhere in its announcements, that it intends to extend this principle to the other provinces which have the same problem, particularly to my own province which has an even greater problem. Nowhere in Canada, and in few places in the world, is road building more essential to the development of the provincial economy, and nowhere is road building more expensive or does it, as a result, place a greater drain on provincial resources. During the past 12 months submissions have been made to the present administration seeking some indication of federal policy either in the fiscal field or through cooperative programs to assist British Columbia as well as other provinces, including Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, in developing a second trans-Canada highway or at least in developing those highways which are neces-


sary to the continuing development of the resources of the western provinces.
I am thinking particularly of the necessity for a highway program linking central British Columbia and the western provinces east of the Rockies to the northern port of Prince Rupert. Canada is a Pacific power. We are apparently coming very reluctantly to a realization that much of Canada's future, much of Canada's growth and much of Canada's prosperity will be dependant upon our relations in the Pacific and the development of trade in that region, matters which in turn are related to a substantial degree to the economic and fiscal help given to the western provinces to enable them to acquire ready access to the west coast ports so as to take full advantage of the markets and services of the Pacific area.
There is at present an intense concentration on the development of facilities in the lower mainland through Vancouver, New Westminster and some of the Vancouver island ports. But one port on the Pacific coast which has received all too little attention over the years is the port of Prince Rupert, which has ready access to the Peace river area and which also has potentially a close link with the city of Edmonton and the economy of northern Alberta.
This is not simply a provincial consideration; it is something which is in the national interest. It comes within the scope of federal participation. It involves the development of facilities on the Pacific coast which will lead to the greater servicing of trade in the Pacific area.
Apart from the trade aspect, we in this house are now considerably concerned with the political situation in the Pacific area. There is conflict there. There has been conflict for years, and there will be conflict for many more years. If it cannot be contained, Canada undoubtedly will be involved. As a Pacific nation it would have no choice. It would be thrust into events even if it did not enter of its own volition. Therefore the development of port facilities on the west coast and transportation through that difficult terrain is of the utmost national importance. However, neither in this mill nor in any announcement which has been made by the government in the past 11 months can I find any sign of any appreciation by the government of this necessity.
There was an announcement made by the Minister of Public Works 53 weeks ago almost precisely, in which he indicated that

Federal-Provincial Relations
some consideration might be given to a national road building program. Then later we heard there would be a stocktaking, and that the provinces would indicate how much it costs to build roads and would be told what they might expect from the federal government. But we heard no more, except that the government was considering the situation, gathering information and filing it. That is all we heard. This is not encouraging at a time when there is a tremendous potential for development in the whole of the Pacific region, including trade with the west coast of the United States and the coast of Alaska, and increasing trade with Australia and New Zealand. The whole of the Pacific region lies open to Canada providing the facilities of the west coast are adequately developed to serve the growing needs of that region.
I believe there is immediacy here. The province of British Columbia recently announced that it was extending its provincial ferry system from Port Hardy to Prince Rupert, from the northern tip of Vancouver island to Prince Rupert, and a connecting highway link would add substantially to the economy of Vancouver island.
The benefit to be gained from federal participation in this type of program is tremendous. I am asking for such participation specifically for British Columbia because of the very special and urgent needs of that province, but I realize as well that a program of this kind embodied in legislation like this could be of immense benefit not only to British Columbia but to all the western provinces, and by benefiting all the western provinces would lead to benefits throughout the whole of Canada. Anyone who has travelled on our national highway system in the last year or two is conscious of the way in which Canadians are travelling and visiting the various provinces. There is a great interchange of people. It is as common now to see Quebec and Ontario licence plates in Vancouver as it was common to see California licence plates. Eastern Canada has suddenly discovered western Canada, and western Canadians are here in the east in the thousands each summer because of one highway network, one cost sharing agreement for highway construction which has brought about this great interchange of people within Canada.
Now we must go further. We must recognize that this has been a good thing and, if the federal government will enter into agreements with the provinces to assist them this tendency can be increased and we can go
a step further. The national government by co-operating with the western provinces, particularly with the province of British Columbia, in the development of highway access to the coast and port facilities on the coast will provide for Canada a new horizon on the Pacific. We can take advantage of the situation. It is there for us to gain. It is there for the taking provided there is some willingness on the part of the federal government to enter into agreements with the western provinces in particular to develop the necessary facilities that will give Canada its opportunity in the Pacific.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise particularly to protest the taxation arrangement involving the use of a gross figure for natural resources rather than a net figure. I think it is only fair to say that the action of the government in this regard has been very discriminatory, and in the few minutes I will take of the committee's time I hope to point out some of the reasons why I make this statement.
I am particularly interested in expressing my views with relation to the forestry industry of British Columbia, which does in fact provide a large return in gross revenue to the province. This is not the case as far as net revenue is concerned, because throughout almost the whole of the province we have established a sustained yield program which is very costly and extends far into the future. It is an investment in the future of British Columbia and Canada. It is an investment on the part of Canadians living today that will be beneficial to those who will follow us.
In the forest industry a tremendous amount of money has to be expended on reforestation and nurseries for the growing of trees. A great deal of money has to be spent every year for forest fire protection. In that connection there are extensive programs involving roads that have to be built, water supplies that have to be maintained and the hiring of aircraft under contract for the whole season whether or not the aircraft are used. The aircraft must be available and have to be paid for in case we have a season with many forest fires. All these expenses have to be met in connection with the forest service.
Forest access roads also have to be built. When we build forest access roads we naturally open up the country for travellers, and this increases the fire hazard. Therefore the amount of fire protection has to be considerably extended because of the number of people using these access roads, and the cost of such protection is increased. These services

Federal-Provincial Relations all cost a lot of money and therefore reduce substantially the amount of net revenue obtained from the forest industry.
A great deal of money also has to be spent both privately and publicly on forest research. There is also the cost of collecting revenue for the government. As any government knows, the money that is received is not a net figure. There is a cost involved in collecting the revenue. These things are not taken into consideration.
Generally I should like to mention the cost of services in British Columbia. The province is one where wages are relatively high, which is a good thing, and it has a high standard of living, which is also a good thing. We appreciate these things and we want to maintain high wages and a good standard of living. There is also the fact that we have a good climate in British Columbia which every year causes an influx of unemployed people from every part of Canada. This influx of unemployed people is no advantage to British Columbia. It is costly to the province to have these unemployed people there seeking work because they find it is much easier to live in a warm climate with limited funds. Many dollars have to be spent on these people in welfare payments. This again is an added expense to a growing province that is moving forward economically.
The increase in the population of British Columbia clearly indicates that this is true. The higher wages result in the federal government receiving a greater amount of personal income tax from those people who are earning their dollars in British Columbia. This, of course, results in added revenue to the federal government without any relation to the wages paid in other parts of Canada or the income of people in other parts of Canada. Here again we are penalized.
We are penalized in another way as well. I refer to the fact that if industries can find a place where wages are lower they will gravitate to that area if it is possible to do so. Therefore in the type of legislation now before us a province that is trying to increase the standard of living of its people and develop the province is being penalized. Legislation of this type will discourage a province from making progress and encourage other provinces to sit idly by and reap the benefits of the development of neighbouring provinces. This type of thing is certainly discriminatory and I believe should be taken into consideration.
The fact that we in British Columbia have higher incomes is evidenced by the fact that in the year just past British Columbia bought


$660 million worth of goods from Ontario and Quebec alone. That is a very sizeable purchase and would not have been possible were it not for the fact that the people in the western provinces have high incomes and are able to spend the money they have earned. Of course the necessary capital expenditure in the province, along with the production of goods and services, has resulted in this type of increase in the money supply for the federal government. All this I have mentioned compounds the discrimination of this type of legislation, which includes the gross income from natural resources. It has been pointed out that many of these resources are not renewable resources, and in this particular case we are selling off what might be termed a capital asset.
Some mention has been made of highway construction in Canada and I would go along with the minister this far, that as long as the fiscal arrangements with the provinces are such that they will permit the provinces to take their responsibility in connection with highway construction I see no real reason why the federal government should get into extensive highway construction. Aside from that, there is a general responsibility on the part of the federal government in connection with highway construction which should be based, as the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstolce said, on a sound, predetermined policy, not on a haphazard sort of policy which is really not a policy at all but merely a matter of saying "There is a great need here; let us jump in and help build a highway"; or, as the hon. member put it, it is the squeaking wheel which gets the grease.
With regard to sales tax paid by the federal government to provinces which levy a sales tax, here again there is a discrimination against those provinces which do not have such a tax, which discrimination should be eliminated. In the first place, if the federal government engages in extensive construction programs in a province which are liable to sales tax, the province concerned gets a double benefit; it gets the benefit of the expenditures of the federal government within the province and it also gets the benefit of the collection of sales tax. That is certainly discriminatory, and there should be compensation to provinces who do not receive this benefit.
The Minister of Finance can enter the picture very substantially in one respect. This is now the case to a degree and I hope it will be a continuing policy. That is, he can use the increase in the money supply as a means

of revenue. By this I mean that the Bank of Canada should supply the increase in the money supply which is necessary, and this money supply could be used for social and public capital spending. This would reduce the amount of pressure which would be put on the provinces and thereby bring about a reduction in taxation. I am sure the minister would agree with this although he will not admit that some of the things are needed that we would like to see.
We placed some questions before the minister during the previous debate, and I noticed a great reluctance on the part of my hon. friend to answer them. I hope before the session ends the estimates of his department will be up for review in sufficient time to allow the minister to answer some of these questions, instead of bringing them forward in the dying moments of the session. I think it is quite important to realize that in a developing and growing country there has to be an increase in the money supply from year to year, and there is no reason why this increase in the money supply should not be brought forth by the Bank of Canada on behalf of the government by way of expenditure on social and capital needs.
I should like to make one last plea, Mr. Speaker, for consideration to be given to the matters which have been raised in this debate in connection with discrimination. I hope we will find that these discriminatory policies will be eliminated. Surely if there is one thing we need in Canada today in talking about Canadian unity, or a united Canada, or a confederation which is going to work, it is a government which will get away from discriminatory policies and institute a broad policy which is good for all Canadians everywhere.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on listening to the hon. member for Cariboo, whose office is next door to mine, I was a little afraid that he had seen what I am going to say to the house today. However, I feel there are some points which I might still emphasize which I hope will be of interest to the Minister of Finance. I did speak briefly on the resolution stage of this bill, and I should like to emphasize some points I brought out.
I would again emphasize that I agree with the principle of tax abatement. I think all of us do. I feel it is a principle which is recognized as fair throughout the dominion, and as long as it is fair we are for it. Generosity in general is something of which we all approve provided it does not ruin the
Federal-Provincial Relations donor in the process. This situation with which we are faced in Bill No. C-lll is very complicated, and I definitely feel that the bill requires revision before the house endorses it.
I am naturally particularly concerned with the welfare of my own province of British Columbia. It is a province which is still largely undeveloped. As previous speakers have mentioned, especially the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke and just now the hon. member for Cariboo, we have large expenditures facing our province. These large expenditures will develop resources which will bring more revenue to the federal treasury. The situation is simply this, that we are concerned at the suggestion that 50 per cent of our income from natural resources will be taken by the federal government out of the treasury of the province.
As we all appreciate, natural resources in many cases are expendable resources and must be maintained if we are to have any future prosperity. We cannot allow these resources to be used up, or allow 50 per cent of the revenue from them to be handed over to the federal government for use in other ways. I feel any suggested assessment in this bill should be applied fairly. I agree with what the hon. member for Cariboo has said, and I am sure no one in this house can disagree with him, that the method of assessing industry on gross income rather than on net income is ridiculous. I intend for my purposes to use the same example used by the hon. member for Cariboo. I am using that example because the forestry industry is the largest in British Columbia and requires great emphasis. Other resources in British Columbia such as oil, gas and mining should naturally be treated in the same way, but I feel that an examination of the forestry industry will give us the best example.
We know that forestry products depend on the forestry industry and must be maintained in perpetuity, otherwise a great deal of our income will disappear. It is only common business sense to protect this industry. It is of interest to note that the forestry industry in British Columbia produces an income of approximately $850 million per annum, and that the maintenance of the forests on a high grade basis is being carried out mainly by private industry.
The forests which come under the jurisdiction of the provincial department of forestry amount to 83 per cent of the forest acreage in British Columbia. It is impossible to maintain those forests out of revenue that is being pro-

Federal-Provincial Relations vided from forestry income. At the present time in the coast area alone there are 100,000 acres of forest land underdeveloped, and in the interior where the forestry industry is developing rapidly this situation is even worse.
People all over British Columbia want roads, schools, hospitals and social services. These are excellent things, and I would be the last man to stand here and argue that they should not be provided. These people want these things because they can see where the money is being spent. On the other hand, money spent in respect of forestry preservation cannot be seen, and in this regard this industry is in an unfavourable position. The federal government through its Department of Forestry contributes toward the maintenance of forests in British Columbia under the provisions of the reforestation act of 1949. The government participates in inventory, the building of protection roads, and reforestation. This system is not working fairly. The federal treasury contributes only 15 per cent of the cost of these services, whereas 85 per cent is being paid by the provincial treasury. However, in respect of services such as the provision of hospitals and welfare the government has seen fit to contribute 50 per cent of the cost.
The forestry industry creates a great deal of income, and if we reinvest this income more industry and more income will be produced. More pulp mills could be created as a result of which there would be a natural increase in income. I am sure the Minister of Finance and the minister of revenue would be pleased to know of the possible development of ten or 20 more pulp mills in British Columbia, because the federal treasury would receive 11 per cent tax on the machinery and buildings.
Several years ago Mr. Justice Sloan conducted an inquiry in respect of the development of forestry in British Columbia. At page 417 of his report regarding this British Columbia industry he indicates that one third of the provincial tax in British Columbia is related to the forestry industry, and that one third of the amount received through the federal tax rental agreement is derived from the forestry industry development. The report also indicates that 26 per cent of total federal revenue from British Columbia is derived from forestry. In other words, out of the revenue from the forestry industry in British Columbia during the past year it is estimated that the province of British Columbia has received $116,500,000. On the other

hand the federal treasury has received $157 million. In other words the federal treasury receives 60 per cent of the revenue of a British Columbia development. The British North America Act on the other hand indicates that a province is responsible for resources and must maintain those resources. Under the tax agreement the federal government only maintains this resource to the extent of 2J per cent.
The province of British Columbia must maintain the forestry industry or become another part of Canada dependent upon subsidization. A more extensive forestry industry must be developed, and the $117 million in tax must be protected. At the present time only 8J per cent of the total income is put back into development, study and fire protection in respect of this industry in British Columbia. The British Columbia government devotes 15 per cent of its income to these services, whereas the federal government contributes only 2J per cent.
If we do not protect this industry; if we allow all the profit to be taken out of forestry production, eventually we will kill the goose that laid the golden egg. We must put more money into forestry development. We must put more money into forestry protection. We must provide better headquarters establishments for these services in the districts which have been opened up in British Columbia. To properly service these headquarters in respect of the forestry industry will cost a great deal of money. It is estimated that $450,000 will be required for buildings alone in new areas necessary for the development of this industry. The federal government is only contributing 2\ per cent toward the cost of construction, reforestation, disease research and research in respect of preservation.
I feel, therefore, that this particular clause in Bill No. C-lll is completely unfair. It is unreasonable and it is unbusinesslike. I feel the minister should give serious consideration to the removal of this provision for imposing a tax on gross income rather than net income. There is no other industry of which I know that is taxed on its gross income. I have never heard of such a thing. I am sure the minister, who has been associated with financial circles in Canada for years, will agree that it is utterly ridiculous to impose a tax on the gross income of any business. Surely to goodness the industry must be maintained, and the net revenue only should be considered when it comes to taxation.
We should encourage these industries to expand because eventually income will be

increased. We should not ruin an industry by taking away more money than we put back into it for its development. No industry can operate on that basis; it will go bankrupt. We all recognize this because it is only ordinary common sense. We should encourage our natural resource development so that we will have more income. We should not discourage it. The present system, especially with regard to forest rehabilitation in British Columbia, is one that will completely discourage the industry in the long run. The only thing that maintains this particular industry in British Columbia is the fact that we are blessed with a great deal of good forest area which we are able to harvest continually without replacement or proper protection. Forestry needs more roads, and this has been dealt with already, Mr. Speaker. Forestry needs more fire protection, more airplanes for fire protection, and this has already been suggested.
I hope I have emphasized the point that you cannot get returns from a business unless you spend money on the development and improvement of that business. This is the point I want to bring home. I am not trying to tell this house that we are not in favour of tax abatement. I am trying to tell this house that tax abatement must be based on the net income of a province and not on the gross income. I think that is only fair; it is only common sense. The remarks 1 have made apply equally to mining and oil production and things of that type.
At the time the resolution was under discussion I asked the minister to give us the assurance that the Columbia river downstream benefits, which result from the sale of a natural resource to the United States, will not be considered a taxable natural resource of the province of British Columbia. This would, of course, completely alter the whole Columbia river treaty. We must not allow that to be included as a natural resource in the consideration of the sale of natural resources so far as British Columbia is concerned.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, this is all I have to say at this time. I am just asking for fair play for British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba or any other province. I am not saying we are the only province affected by this provision. I just want to put this on the record. We must not allow legislation to be passed that deals unfairly with any province. I feel an adjustment must be made in this bill in order that the tax will be imposed on a net basis rather than on the gross.

speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Lethbridge.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just heard something in the house that I have wanted to hear for a long time, and want to hear repeated many times. The hon. member who spoke before me said something to the effect that Quebec will always benefit by belonging to confederation. As a western member I would like to compliment him for uttering those words and to assure him and others that we feel exactly the same way. We all want to benefit from being in confederation, and those of us who are, comparatively speaking, new members feel this more strongly than a lot of people give us credit for at times.
Dealing with Bill No. C-lll there are one or two items I would like to bring to the attention of the house through you, Mr. Speaker. I have listened to the debate with interest. I have heard much said about federal-provincial problems and about the problems of different provinces. Many discrepancies in fiscal arrangements have been mentioned, but one person has been neglected, or at least has not been mentioned in the speeches previously made. That person is the Canadian taxpayer. He exists under many names. He may be called one thing or another but to me, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Canadian Taxpayer is the one who is really most concerned with this bill. It is not the individual member who speaks, and rightly so, about a grievance concerning a whole province, who is most concerned with this bill; it is the individual taxpayer.
I heard a very eloquent and telling speech by a colleague of mine from Alberta. He is, in a manner of speaking, my neighbour, and he dealt with federal-provincial fiscal arrangements as they relate to taxpayers in Alberta. If I may I would like to dwell on that subject for a few moments and ask questions. Albertans are asking questions locally; they are asking them provincially, and they are asking them federally through their representatives in this chamber. There are two things I have in mind, dealing particularly with the relationship between urban and rural taxpayers.

I could, Mr. Speaker, quote from the Financial Post of August 1, which gives a very optimistic report on business conditions, one that I am sure we all like to see. It carries headlines such as "Barometer Rising"-I presume this refers to the financial barometer- "Jobs Galore," "Builders' Boon," "Strength Overseas", etc. All these things affect the Canadian taxpayer very closely, probably more closely than a lot of us mention or even think about because we are so wrapped up in our own duties here that we often forget this sort of thing.
I would like to draw a comparison between rural and urban taxpayers, and I do this quite sincerely and honestly because I am concerned with both categories. A rural taxpayer may deduct certain expenses for interest rates and certain costs related to his over-all income, and I think it would be a good thing if the urban dweller could be entitled to the same consideration, particularly concerning the cost of interest on mortgage loans as related to the purchase of dwellings. For a long time I have said that there is a discrepancy between these two groups. For instance, if I am on my own farm I am entitled to many more deductions than the city dweller, who does not receive a deduction for the interest rate he pays on the mortgage covering his home. I believe he should be entitled to that deduction and to enjoy all the things that the rural taxpayer enjoys. Then too, as a farmer, if I am not able to pay my taxes and the tax collector finally comes along accompanied by the sheriff, I am dispossessed of my property, and rightly so. I am not complaining about that, but with that goes my livelihood.
The economic barometer, it has been said, is rising, and with it comes the prospect of jobs galore. According to statistics, which no doubt are reliable, six and a half million people are at work today, six and a half million out of approximately 19 million. I do not mean to imply that the remaining 12i million are not taxpayers, but certainly the 6j million who are employed are taxpayers. What do they get for their tax dollar? I think the Canadian taxpayer has a right to know where his tax dollar is going.
I am particularly interested in Alberta, as I said earlier. The government of that province provides its taxpayers with a small piece of paper which sets out in detail each and every grant made to a municipality. This adds up to a great deal of money. As a matter of fact, I think in Alberta at the present time it would probably amount to well over $8 mil-20220-4131
Federal-Provincial Relations lion, perhaps $8,750,000; the figure may not be entirely correct, because I speak from memory. But it is a fact that such details are made known to individual taxpayers and I should like to draw this practice to the attention of hon. members as well as to the attention of Canadian taxpayers generally. In one province, at least, taxpayers receive a piece of paper setting out in detail each and every expenditure by way of grant to a municipal government.
Since this is the case with regard to government expenditures within a certain province, I wonder whether it would not be fair to tell the federal taxpayers what is being done with the tax dollars which go to the federal government. I have in the past objected to this sort of propaganda. I did so because I did not believe it was entirely fair for the provincial taxpayer to be reminded what the provincial government was giving to him when he was not also reminded at the same time of the benefits brought about by certain fiscal relationships between the province and the dominion or central government. It left him wondering what the central government was doing with the money he was paying in federal income tax every year.
The hon. member for Lapointe was among several members who spoke earlier in this debate. I am sorry he is not in his place at the moment, because he had a great deal to say about the federal-provincial relationship. As I recall it, he expressed the view that his province should no longer be placed under any restrictions whatsoever. He said in effect that the relationship between the provincial and the federal governments led him to think of Quebec as being a child in a family. If that is so I should like to ask the hon. member whether he thinks that, in effect the federal government should turn the pay cheque over to the family and say "Do as you like; I will take what is left." Does he not believe that to follow such a course would only lead to a deterioration of the federal-provincial relationship? My own view is that it would be bound to do so.
If I may turn now to the agreements themselves, let me say I am frankly and sincerely of the opinion that though they may not be entirely correct, they are certainly good agreements, as far as possible, between the federal government and the provinces. We could argue for a long time about ways in which they could be improved, but let us remember that the premiers of the ten provinces have sat down time after time together with representatives of the government of Canada to

Federal-Provincial Relations consider these fiscal arrangements conscientiously and to reach agreements which seemed lair to all sides. It is true that I have put forward some criticism, but I do not really question the agreements themselves and, in fact,
I should like to compliment the minister responsible.
Earlier in this debate one hon. member referred to the subject of education. I fully realize that this is definitely a provincial responsibility, and it is one which I hope the provinces will always guard jealously. Nevertheless there may be some possibility of reaching agreement and understanding on a a few points at some future conference, in the same way as understanding and agreement have been reached on various matters in the past. There is one point in particular that I should like to draw to the attention of the house, and it is this; the need for a basic standard of education right across this nation regardless of geographical or economic differences.
I know I am treading on ground here where I have no real right to tread. However, having in mind the rapid transportation and communication facilities which today perform a very good service, although some of them have been under fire in the house recently; having in mind also the amount of the taxpayer's dollar that is funnelled into education in all phases, elementary and intermediate schools and universities, I think it is time that we came to some agreement. It would be my hope that there might at least be agreement on a basic standard. Those members of the house who have children and who come from constituencies far from Ottawa try to meet the very difficult problem that arises.
Our country is nearly 5,000 miles wide and our children move from one province to another or one area of the country to another each year. I have experienced this, and I should like to say that the educational systems with which I have had contact are very close but not quite close enough. There is a difference in the grading. But what is even more disturbing is that in a city such as Ottawa and in my own city-no doubt the same situation exists throughout the country -even when a student moves from one area in the same city to another area in the same city he is very often faced with different textbooks and a different curriculum.
I am not speaking from a selfish point of view or from the federal standpoint at all, but surely in the interests of the Canadian taxpayer we can find some area of agreement
[Mr. Giuidlock.f
regardless of provincial autonomy or any other argument that may be brought forward. Surely we can arrive at very basic standards so that students who move from one area of the country to another or even from one school division to another within the same city will be able to take advantage of the fact that there are basic standards.
Yesterday the hon. member for Lapointe dealt with a matter to which I have taken some exception, but I think I learned something from him yesterday. I am referring to the fact that we in this house often hear about the great breach between the races. I have taken exception to such statements on several occasions in the house, but I think I may have learned something from the hon. member. He pointed out that the definitions of certain words are not the same in the two languages. If I have been mistaken in the past I offer my apologies, but I would like to ask the hon. member to give a clearer definition of these words, because certainly my idea of confederation does not encompass differences between the races.
I hope I am completely mistaken, because when I look at certain members of the house it is very hard for me to realize that we are of different races, and I should like the dictionary definition of these words to be made clear. I said earlier it was my hope that before long we would not be talking about differences of this sort. I have also said that I hope we can have a basic standard of education regardless of geographic or economic differences. When the federal government and the provinces sit down again in conference I think they might consider this matter. If they would do so I am quite sure it would enhance Canada's chances of taking her proper place in the very near future. We must be very cognizant of this, because we have to take our proper place.
I have also referred to the position of the Canadian taxpayer in relation to employment or unemployment. I should like some answer in this regard, because when we are talking about federal-provincial arrangements the Canadian taxpayer is most certainly involved. I think he should receive a full explanation of where his tax dollar goes. I tried to point out earlier that the province of Alberta does a very good job of explaining to the taxpayers where the municipal grants come from, but they do a very poor job of pointing out the differences, which leads the Canadian taxpayer to wonder in some cases, as we have heard during this debate, where the

rest of his tax dollar goes and what is being done with it.
I know some of us would like to think that the gross national product will increase to a point where taxes will not have to be raised in the next budget, but I wonder frankly whether this will really be the case. When I note that six and a half million people work in Canada today it leaves a question in my mind about the other four or five or six million people. Where are they? I realize that we have a great many professional people in Canada who are taxpayers, and in looking over the figures there is a very nice picture. But where are these other people who are worth thinking about and who are really the people concerned about this present debate? Where do they fit into these figures? How many of them really know the answer as to where their tax dollar is going? As I mentioned earlier, some of these people -admittedly I do not know how many-are paying more than other people. I think they have every right to some explanation of where their tax dollar goes.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, the minister will take note of one or two of the matters I have raised and will give some public explanation, or if not public at least give an explanation to this house, in reply.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have an opportunity to say a few words in the house since an unfortunate accident kept me in hospital for a few weeks.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I wish to thank my colleague from Longueuil for this welcome.
I want to tell the house that, although I was kept apart from the debates, I followed with a keen interest all the developments in this house, especially as regards relations between the provinces and the federal government.
I felt somewhat unhappy being unable to take part in the debate on Bill No. C-110 relating to the student loans. I wish to say at this stage that had I been present in the house when that bill was introduced, I would have surely registered my opposition on this question, since I consider that education, as understood by the Fathers of Confederation and sanctioned by the British North America Act, and more especially by sections 92 and 93, comes under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. The more so since I believe this central government, failed to discharge
Federal-Provincial Relations
its responsibilities in the course of the various federal-provincial conferences which were held in Ottawa since its coming into office. This government was certainly made aware, in no uncertain terms, of the stand of the province of Quebec on the question of education. I was told very clearly by several Quebec Liberal ministers that the province of Quebec intends to retain its full authority over the matter of education.
Besides, we are under the impression that the Prime Minister has given way to pressures from his entourage, but mostly to pressures put on him and his ministers by the teachers' federation of Canada through a brief dated November 18, 1963, in which on page 13, it is stated:
The federation of Canadian school teachers does not feel that the Canadian government should control in any way education in our country, but it recommends nevertheless:
The word "nevertheless" is very significant.
That the federal government should take the initiative in calling a representative meeting of ministers of education of every province, their advisers, and representatives of national organizations most directly concerned in order to seek together the means of removing existing difficulties.
In itself, this recommendation seems acceptable, but the fact remains that the spirit and the letter of the confederation pact seem to be completely ignored, because in educational matters, such an initiative must not be taken by the central government, but rather by the provinces themselves. And that is the danger which arises when the federal government takes the initiative in the field of education.
Mr. Speaker, I would not want my observations to be interpreted as separatist or nationalist remarks. Far from it. On the contrary, I am one of those who believe that in Canada, there are 11 equal governments and not that one is superior to the 10 provincial governments. And it is only when we accept that philosophy, those facts, that we will reduce in Canada the number of problems which oppose from time to time the provinces and the central government.
Besides, if the federal government wanted to do so, it could take measures allowing the provinces to discharge their own obligations in that field. But it seems that the federal government always wants to keep the door closed to initiatives which could come directly under the provinces.
For instance, some departments' estimates could be reduced, as pointed out by one of Quebec's most prominent ministers, Mr. Rene Levesque who, as reported in Le Devoir on
6538	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Relations October 22, 1963, recommended that money be invested in education rather than national defence.
That is, in my opinion, a very logical proposal which would be acceptable, because it would take away from the federal government a source of expenditures which, I feel, is used only to increase taxes and which could be put to good use by the provinces in the field of education.
In Le Devoir of December 4, 1964, the editorial writer stated the problem rather clearly. Under the heading:
Provincial needs and military expenses.
Mr. Paul Sauriol stated:
Three days alter the federal-provincial conference, a report from Ottawa indicated that the Department of National Defence had cut some $74 million from its budget for the current year. The federal treasury is thus recovering almost the equivalent of the $87 million turned over to the provinces. There is perhaps no direct connection between both facts, but it is not a mere coincidence, since a great number of people believe that the most efficient and logical way to satisfy provincial claims is to reduce considerably our military expenditures.
A little further, Mr. Sauriol wrote:
In August 1962, Mr. Diefenbaker added to the austerity program announced a few weeks earlier by cutting defence expenditures by $100 million. Outlays are nevertheless $1,576 million but, since there has been an increase in the meantime, total spending in that connection will be reduced to 1,560 this year.
Consequently, if the government truly wished to solve the problem of education, it could imitate the former Prime Minister and take up the suggestions made by the provincial premiers who advocated a cut in certain government expenditures which are not really essential so that the provinces might get the funds they absolutely need for education.
In fact, there are several means the federal government could take to allow the provinces to recover the money they need for education. But I wonder why the present government persists in refusing to amend the Criminal Code so that the provinces that may wish to do so could set up a lottery program and use the profits therefrom for educational purposes.
Mr. Speaker, why that request is being repeatedly turned down is beyond me, since the province of Quebec has already declared itself in favour of such a project in the proportion of 87 per cent, following a public opinion poll throughout the province. Besides, two of the more recent premiers of the province, that is, Mr. Lesage and Mr. Duplessis,


made such a request to the central government.
Besides, during the last election campaign, the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Rouleau) formally stated that if their party was elected they would see to it that the Criminal Code be amended in order to legalize the holding of lotteries in the provinces. That would be a means for the provinces to finance their education requirements.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must tell the hon. member that I was sick in one leg, but not in the head, as might be the case with the hon. member for Lotbiniere.
Mr. Speaker, other means are available to the central government to find formulas which would be acceptable to the provinces, while respecting fully the spirit and the letter of the confederation pact, with regard to education which is strictly a matter of provincial jurisdiction. I am thinking, for instance, of a step which could be taken by the provinces: until such time when the central government would give back to the provinces the rights of direct taxation to which they are entitled under the B.N.A. Act, organizations could be set up which would make it possible for the

provinces to meet their obligations in the field of education.
But I think that, in the meantime, the provinces could undertake to set up an interprovincial council for university grants.
You are no doubt aware that England, after the second world war, created a sort of council for university grants. The council is above politics and serves only as liaison between the government and the universities. But it nevertheless has the power to conduct inquiries in all universities in the country, assess their needs and point out to the government the amount the universities need to discharge their responsibilities. Then the government approves a budget based on the requirements submitted by the council.
The provinces might set up themselves a council which would be somewhat based on the same principle and which would be non-political. This council might include one representative per province, appointed by the government of course, and another representative from the business world. It might thus voice the views of Canadian institutions to their government which, in turn, would present to the federal government the needs of universities.
The sums of money given this way, according to the evaluations of this council, would then be handed out to the provinces, which would distribute them; this would be in accordance with the spirit and the letter of the confederation pact of 1867.
Mr. Speaker, the education question is obviously not the only one that can be raised during this debate on Bill No. C-lll.
We have now the opportunity to find out what created uneasiness for a number of years between the government of Canada and the provincial governments.
In respect to the relations between the provinces and the federal government, I should like to say that I deplore the fact that quite often when we speak about these relations, we tend to make faulty comparisons; for instance, someone suggested that the federal government and the provinces should have father-and-son relations. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, there are no father-and-son relations between the federal government and the provincial governments, but instead there should be brother-and-brother relations, so that they may discuss on an equal basis.
I also think that, as a member from the province of Quebec, I should say that there is no serious dispute between the province of Quebec and the other provinces of Canada.
Federal-Provincial Relations As the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gre-goire) said yesterday, the word "racial" is sometimes differently interpreted by our English speaking fellow members and those who are French speaking.
But there is rather a problem of provincial claims on the central government, because of the difficulties which each province has in settling its own problems, in the field of education, health or any other field, which come under exclusive provincial jurisdiction.
And, here, I think I may quote a view of the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve)-now vacationing on the French Riviera or at Capri -who, when he was on the job, made certain statements which should hold our attention.
On November 6, 1963, according to Le Devoir, the present Minister of Forestry said during a talk he gave in Montreal:
The marked uneasiness in Quebec is due to economic factors.
And he added:
It is up to the federal government to "save confederation" by enacting legislation which will reduce unemployment and raise the living standard of the people in Quebec. A step in the right direction has already been taken by the Liberal government-
I wonder what step, as unemployment has risen in the province of Quebec, and more particularly in Montreal, where there are 1700 more unemployed than last year.
The article says further:
When taking part in a discussion on unemployment in the House of Commons, the Montreal economist noted that the unemployment level in Quebec was much higher than in Ontario, and that the opposite was the case with regard to the per capita income.
And further on:
Mr. Sauv6 stressed that the majority of Quebeckers are nationalist in that sense, but that only the "majority" is separatist-

speechtext: The minority.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS

Of course, the minority.
The hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine charged his English speaking fellow citizens with mistaking Quebec nationalism for separatism. By that very fact, English speaking Canadians ignore the facts and jeopardize national unity.
The hon. member was not yet a minister when he made such statements.
The Liberal member of parliament called for a closer co-operation between the federal government and the provinces with regard to steps likely to check unemployment.
This man, when he was a private Liberal member, acknowledged the existence of unemployment, in spite of promises of full employment made by his party during election campaigns.

Federal-Provincial Relations
Mr. Sauve added:
Provincial governments are in a better position than the central government to deal with local economic problems.
Those are the words of man considered within the Liberal party as a first-rate economist, even though he prefers to take holidays instead of carrying out his parliamentary duties.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Here is a man who is now a minister and who is saying to the federal cabinet:
Provincial governments are in a better position than the central government to deal with local economic problems.
Despite that assertion made by the Minister of Forestry, despite that warning from his colleagues, the Minister of Finance introduced Bill No. C-110 and Bill No C-lll, the second of which is contrary to the thinking of the Minister of Forestry and constitutes also a further obstacle to the good relations that should exist between the provinces and the central government.
Moreover, opinions expressed by various Canadian newspapers are favourable to provincial autonomy in several fields. I hope the central government will realize it cannot be the master of destinies in Canada, but that it ought to be the collaborator, with the provinces, in the development of an economic policy set down, not according to the co-operative federalism formula, which I feel is but a smokescreen for greater centralization, but in a spirit of close co-operation between the central government and the provinces, as regards the rights and prerogatives provided for in the British North America Act of 1867.
To show how better co-operation between the central authorities and the provinces would be the solution, it is essential to point out certain statements made in Canadian newspapers.
Among others, I would like to quote an article by Mr. Vincent Prince published in La Presse, on Wednesday, November 27, 1963 under the title:
Very fine plea by Mr. Lesage- in which Mr. Prince stated the following:
In fact considering their revenues, the provinces have effectively spent more than the federal authorities since 1954. As a result, their debts have increased by almost 50 per cent, while those of Ottawa only increased by 22.8 per cent.
In my opinion, this is the crucial point of the trouble facing the provinces in their relations with the federal government. While the

provinces have greater obligations in the field of education, road communications, health, etc., the federal government, with lesser obligations, has taken for itself taxation fields on a much higher scale than was needed.
We are told that provincial expenses have increased by 50 per cent, while the expenses of the federal government have increased by only 22 per cent. It seems to me that it would be normal for the central government, if it wanted to be really honest in its relations with the provinces, to yield not to political representations, but to priority rights that the provinces have outlined to the Ottawa authorities during federal-provincial conferences.
Despite the fact that Premier Lesage of the province of Quebec has mentioned priority needs, in my opinion there are indeed priority rights. One of those priority rights is the authority of a province to collect taxes for purposes which are a definite provincial responsibility.
Moreover, all enlightened people, economists, like the Minister of Forestry, as well as financiers, except perhaps the federal government, are of the opinion that there should be a better distribution of taxes in Canada.
And it should be noted that I object to the pretense that there must be a strong federal government and ten provincial governments under its control.
This is a false conception which is contrary to the views expressed by the Minister of Justice in a speech he recently delivered in Montreal when he said-and here the Minister of Justice and myself perhaps agree, as well as Quebec and the other provinces: We must realize that there are in Canada 11 governments which have equal rights within their own jurisdiction and which can negotiate on an equal footing.
But if we accept the theory that there must be one superior government and ten inferior governments, then we are sustaining the very antithesis of the spirit of the confederation pact because when the pact was signed in 1867 it was agreed that henceforth we were to become equal partners within an administration which would recognize the rights conferred under the pact.
Over the years, the centralizing spirit developed to such an extent that, during the war, we agreed to the theory of a strong central government, in view of the fact that our country was at war and that emergency measures had to be taken; and in the circumstances, the government had to ensure the security of Canada at any cost. But, due

to the war, or rather to these agreements made in time of war, the central government grabbed more rights belonging to provinces, under the terms of an agreement respecting tax rentals.
We recall only too well how easily Mr. Godbout voluntarily and quickly yielded the rights of the province of Quebec to the federal government of the time, which was headed by the Right Hon. Mackenzie King.
Those tax-rental agreements were supposed to be temporary and in effect only during the war, but they still exist.
That is why in certain provinces, and particularly in the province of Quebec, problems arose because of inadequate revenues from direct taxation.
All the premiers who have headed the province of Quebec have claimed the taxation fields which belong to the province. First of all, Mr. Duplessis, then Mr. Sauve and finally Mr. Lesage. Mr. Lesage even served an ultimatum to the present government to yield to the representations of the province of Quebec, otherwise the province would take other drastic measures.
For those who denied that Mr. Lesage had given such an ultimatum-I remember that the Prime Minister as well as other ministers in this cabinet denied that Mr. Lesage had given the central government an ultimatum-[DOT] there is but one thing to do and it is to read the monthly bulletin issued by the Banque Canadienne Nationale in May 1963; on page 2 of this bulletin, reference is made to Mr. Lesage's ultimatum.
Those people are not politicians but business men, and I suggest that they are as honest as our friends opposite.
Now, in this bulletin, under the heading:
Mr. Lesage's ultimatum-
One can read:
The financial difficulties confronting the province of Quebec stem mainly from the fact that, since the end of the war, Ottawa has invaded many fields, this action resulting in increased taxes, especially direct taxes. That fiscal field, granted the provinces by the constitution, has become nearly exclusively federal property. All the political parties represented in parliament continue, at every election, to make promises which, if implemented, would put a heavier burden on the Canadian taxpayer. The federal government should put off such and such project, even give up certain responsibilities-education, for instance-which, by their very nature, come under the provinces. The most urgent needs, apart from those concerning national defence, are the responsibility of the provinces and the municipalities.
These things have not been said by political organizations but by businessmen who, in my 20220-414
Federal-Provincial Relations opinion, deserve our respect and our consideration.
This article goes on as follows:
The presence of Liberal governments in Quebec and in Ottawa complicates the situation. Before the election of April 5 last, Mr. Lesage stated that only the party under the leadership of Mr. Lester Pearson offered adequate guarantee for the province of Quebec's fiscal autonomy.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
I hear my hon. friend from Lotbiniere applauding.
Since then, we have deceived him, because the Liberal government has voted the student loans act.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I see those people approving intrusions in the educational field which strictly come under provincial jurisdiction.
Another federal intrusion is that of loans to municipalities which have been denounced by the Quebec premier, Mr. Lesage, and by Mr. Laporte, minister of municipal affairs.
That is what makes relations so tense between the federal government and the provinces in Canada. Some people are willing to sacrifice the rights guaranteed by an unalterable pact, the confederation act, in order to toe the party line.
Mr. Speaker, the public and the provincial governments have, for the past several years, been constantly reminded of such federal encroachments.
In that connection, I should like to quote an article which appeared in La Presse. I choose a newspaper which is friendly to the Liberals, because it is even more conclusive. The article in question written by Mr. Vincent Prince on February 26, 1964, reads as follows:
"Infringement by consent?"
Could it be that under the cover of "co-operative federalism", Ottawa is trying to impose "infringement by consent" upon us?
This query is perhaps not as futile as it may seem at first sight. At least, to those who may for some time have observed the central government's activities.
We may simply recall last year's legislation authorizing Ottawa to grant municipal loans. We might, more particularly, consider the federal bill now before the house and which, this time, concerns financial aid to students.
In our humble opinion, this is not co-operation of a federalist character, but an infringement on that very federalism-
That, I think, proves what this central government, and perhaps the former administrations, do not want to understand that national unity would benefit if doors, and

Federal-Provincial Relations minds, were open not only to a sincere discussion but to an honest and practical observance of provincial claims.
The provincial governments have problems of their own. In Quebec, we have, and will have, more than in the other provinces where the problems are perhaps less complicated, except in Ontario. Each province must, therefore enjoy the entire possession of its sources of revenue required for the proper administration of the public weal and the discharge of its responsibilities in matters of education, health and in other fields which are under exclusively provincial jurisdiction according to the terms of the confederation pact. Only such a spirit can prevent certain radical elements in the provinces of Quebec from extending their venture into the field of separatism, something which would have damaging effects for Canada.
But I feel that the one to blame, should such a situation materialize, will be the present central government. Indeed, it has been told about that kind of situation by its own ministers, by the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), the man responsible for the fact that the Liberals of Mr. Lesage and Mr. Levesque have been elected in the province of Quebec. As I say, those people have made the present central government aware of the serious problems now facing Quebec but which the central government refuses to recognize or to take seriously, inasmuch as, through the strength of its majority and perhaps with the co-operation of certain minor opposition parties, it insists on passing Bill No. C-110 and Bill No. C-lll.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I did say minor parties, which will disappear anyway in the next election, and this will benefit Canada as a whole.
I hope the central government will try, at the next premiers' conference, to understand that it is not simply with magic formulas, such as the co-operative federalism formula which was suggested by the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne), but rather with practical solutions, through the central government becoming conscious of the fact that it must withdraw from the taxation fields reserved to the provinces, that the problem will be solved.
It is by this means only that we shall succeed in achieving strong provinces, provincial governments as strong as the central government, and such co-operation will occur only

if there exists good will on the part of the central government.
Now, in conclusion, I wish to state that I object-and I wish to register my objection since I had no opportunity to do this sooner- to this Bill No. C-110, which I consider as an interference in a strictly provincial field. I urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) to stop such encroachments, such intrusions in fields of provincial jurisdiction and to provide practical consideration for the problems raised or the representations made by the premiers of the provinces.
