maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
take this opportunity to express some real fears concerning the course this government is taking with regard to federal-provincial relations, particularly as related to the bill before us. My conclusion, which I will state at the beginning as well as at the end of my remarks, is that the government is, through its actions, contributing beyond doubt to the separation of this country into two parts.
This is happening in two ways. The first is obvious; it is a direct method. The other, the indirect method which is less obvious, is one having to do with financial measures. It is this aspect of federal-provincial affairs I should like to deal with today because it lies at the very heart of the bill we are considering. I wish to deal with financial arrangements as they concern the increasing difficulties which have arisen between the province of Quebec and the rest of Canada. I say at once that I am a believer in "one Canada", albeit a changing Canada. As I understand confederation, it was something of an agreement between a number of provinces-something very much in the nature of a contract. One term of the contract was spelled out very clearly at that time. It was that certain matters should lie solely within the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. There were reasons for making these reservations at the time, and some of them are still valid.

In particular the provinces, especially the province of Quebec, insisted that questions concerning education and public welfare, among other things, would be decided by the provinces.
It may be that the national picture has changed since the time of confederation, and perhaps we ought to recognize this. But we must first of all recognize that the contract which was made at that time still stands, valid and unamended, and we must not continually make demands on the provinces for parts of their jurisdiction unless there has been unanimous agreement beforehand. The bill before us relates directly to the youth allowances bill as well as to certain other fiscal arrangements. Perhaps I might just for a moment examine the legislative proposals which have preceded this measure and which are along the same lines. We have already this session passed the youth allowances bill and the student loans bill. We have also had the Canada pension bill before us on at least two occasions. Here are three bills, all brought forward by the present government, which have followed a pattern. I do not say this pattern has been followed intentionally, but I do assert that, intentionally or unintentionally, they have brought about a result which is most undesirable in Canada. These three bills I have mentioned have one thing in common. They all invade the provincial field to a degree, some more than others, regardless of whether or not that was the intention of the government.
Some people in English speaking parts of Canada find it difficult to understand how the youth allowances bill might be considered as invading the provincial sphere of responsibility with regard to education. Yet I have heard many of my colleagues explain why Canadians in the province of Quebec feel that it is an invasion of provincial rights, basically because it influences the priorities which the province has to set up and in respect of which it must apply provincial revenues. In all these bills there has been an invasion of provincial rights to the point which one province, the province of Quebec, has said: No, we will not agree; you will have to make some other arrangement. This is not what I would call unanimous prior consent. All it amounts to is an agreement that the other nine provinces are to be allowed to take advantage of the legislation if they wish to, while Quebec declines to have any part of it. To this extent the situation does not meet the requirement I have men-20220-414J
Federal-Provincial Relations tioned, namely that there should be prior unanimous agreement.
I do not think we can blame the provinces if they complain about an invasion of their provincial rights. This applies to other provinces besides Quebec. However it is the province of Quebec which has raised the greatest objection, and it is the province of Quebec which is the subject of discussions and talk about separation. I think therefore that we must consider how this legislation affects that province, in particular. I would say that the continual invasion of provincial rights by this government in its controversial and somewhat ineffective legislation is making a farce out of confederation as it was designed in 1867. This situation is being brought about without any effort to get together with the provinces and say: Conditions in Canada have changed; we must recognize this; we must hold a conference to see whether, perhaps, at university level there might be some federal control in the field of education.
These things should be discussed as a preliminary, before the government considers the unfortunate invasions it has been making into provincial fields. I am not putting up a case for the provinces, or for the province of Quebec in particular. That is not what I am here for. But I want to follow up these comments with the conclusion I have reached, namely that the nine provinces which accept these proposals by the federal government are tending to form one bloc, or one group of Canadians to whom certain legislation applies, while on the other hand we have the province of Quebec standing alone as the one province which has not taken part in these programs-the province which has declined to accept the legislation I have mentioned. The nine provinces are tending to surrender to the central government in Ottawa powers which are traditionally theirs. Quebec says, in effect, that none of these programs shall apply in that province. Thus a situation is developing which really concerns me, since we are bringing about a de facto separation of this country into two groups within the framework of confederation-within the framework of one Canada in which all the provinces are supposed to have equal rights.
I say that we should face the problem directly at a conference, as has been suggested many times, to consider the changing conditions in Canada and to come to some agreement on the particularly sensitive problems of welfare and education. If we cannot reach

Federal-Provincial Relations any agreement we should stop breaking up the country by trying to invade these fields. Second, if we cannot reach any understanding on this matter we should make payments of money in the nature of grants in lieu of these programs, and leave the programs alone. We should increase the tax fields of the provinces and make larger grants to the provinces.
It has been stated by several hon. members that there is no point in increasing the tax fields of the provinces if they are poor provinces and just do not have the money. This is a waste of effort because it is only a larger percentage of nothing. As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) pointed out last night, the percentage in one or two of the provinces is zero minus, because they are receiving more from the federal government than is being collected in taxes within those provinces. Therefore to increase the share of taxation would not bring about the result. What we have to do if we have to have these national problems is to leave alone the question of making two rules for two different groups of Canadians and design, if we must, a different system of tax sharing within this country.
I will admit that education has now become a matter of national concern. I think that many people both inside and outside the house feel that the federal government should take an interest in and become a part of the educational field in Canada, most particularly at the senior levels. From what I can understand as the result of inquiries, this is a subject which, at the university level, might certainly be open to discussion with the province of Quebec. If it were, perhaps the great need we have in science and other related fields for the ability to be educated in one part of Canada and to take postgraduate work in another might be met. I believe this is something we must consider, but we cannot do it by the backdoor method as we are doing now and continue to keep this country together.
I should like to quote an hon. member with whom I have never found myself in agreement, but who pointed out something that is in line with what I am saying now.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: To whom is the hon. member referring?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
It is not the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) but the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). That hon. member says: "Let this happen; I like to see it." I say it is happening but it should not. Nevertheless we both have the same idea as to what is happening. When we

were considering the student loan legislation he said, as found on page 5932 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that more and more such bills will be introduced in the House of Commons and that more and more the federal government will try to control all the jurisdiction possible in the nine English speaking provinces, so that, more and more, the nine provincial governments will have nothing to do and we may see their consolidation in the hands of the Ottawa government, whereas, at the same time, the province of Quebec will withdraw from all those joint plans and will administer its affairs by herself. So, before long, we shall have only two governments in Canada: the Ottawa government for the nine English speaking provinces and the Quebec government for the province of Quebec. We will then achieve what I forecast yesterday: two governments only, two states, not separated but associated.
I do not agree with this as an objective, Mr. Speaker. I could not disagree more strongly. Nevertheless I do say that this is the effect and result of the types of legislation that have been introduced at this session. It is something that causes me a great deal of concern because, perhaps by an indirect method, perhaps by an imperceptible method and perhaps unintentionally, we have drifted into a situation now where, with regard to almost half of the legislation that is introduced, one of the provinces says: We will not become involved in this; you can do what you like; give us the money instead and we will use it the way we want to.
If it is logical for one province to do this, surely it is logical for the others. I merely say that the government should not be continually embarrassing the provinces and this house by introducing the type of legislation which is achieving this result. I ask myself why the premier of Quebec is constantly raising objections to certain measures, such as the three pieces of legislation I have mentioned, to such an extent that the federal government says: All right, you do not have to come in; we will give you some money instead. I do not think it is particularly because he wants more money although I am sure every province does. I think the premier of the province of Quebec sees what is happening and understands these joint plans are leading to a situation that he would like to see, namely a Quebec which is not just a province of the country but is a separate and strong part of the country.
We in English speaking Canada have to admit that Quebec is not a province like the others. This is an obvious fact not often understood. It is obvious because if it had not been that Quebec was different we would not have confederation as it was formed in 1867. If we had been all the same we could

have agreed on everything and would not have had to have a separation of powers. Quebec is different, but in recognizing this we must not fall into the trap that I think is now being laid, to have us recognize that it is different in a different way from what it was understood to be at the time of confederation.
The Fathers of Confederation said: There are certain rights you will have as a province along with all the other provinces. They said: Each province shall have the same rights as all the other provinces and the federal government shall have those rights that the provinces do not specifically require. This is understandable. This is the basis of confederation. We have gone along on this basis now for nearly 100 years. But this is not the type of confederation into which we are drifting today. We are drifting into a confederation where reference is not made to all the provinces but where it is said that Quebec is entitled to certain things and the rest of the country must join with the federal government to make a separate block.
This is the great fear that I have from watching pieces of legislation as they come in, particularly the Canada pension plan, and I will certainly have more to say about that when it comes forward for debate. This is the direction into which the whole matter is drifting. Perhaps some other provinces will opt out of the pension plan, and frankly I would not blame them; but this is all part of the same picture.
However, Mr. Speaker, having said that I must also say that I will have to support this bill because it is necessary to the implementation of other legislation which we have already passed. We have passed the Youth Allowance Act, and clause 6 of this bill and following are necessary to follow up that act. Therefore I cannot vote against the bill because it is necessary to legislation we have already passed. However, this indicates the problem we are facing in our national life, that we take one step here and then have to take another step in another direction in consequence, and gradually we find ourselves taking steps to the side rather than ahead.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I hope we have seen the last of this type of divisive legislation. I think there is hope that this sort of drifting to which I have referred is becoming perceptible to the members of the government and that they are beginning to see what they are doing by bringing in this sort of legislation without unanimous agreement. Surely the government
Federal-Provincial Relations can now see the direction in which they are going, whether it be intended or accidental. In any event, I trust this will be the last bill which is brought in under which one province can declare itself excepted from its provisions while the others are included.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this has been a rather prolonged debate. We have gone through the resolution stage and are now on second reading. I think that some of those pundits who say that parliament has deteriorated and is no longer the body it was at one time should read some of the speeches which have been made during the course of the resolution debate and now on second reading, which I think have been at a very high level and reflect credit upon the parliament of Canada. I deprecate any suggestion that parliament has deteriorated, because when one goes back over the problem, which is not a new one-as I will suggest in a moment or two it goes back to my own province, from whence it originated-he realizes that it has been with us for almost a century. I suggest that the debates which have taken place on this particular bill on the matter of dominion-provincial relations compare favourably with debates which have taken place at any time heretofore.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, the debate has been prolonged, but the subject with which we are dealing is most important. I do not intend to take the time of the house by going into too much detail with regard to these matters, albeit that there are some complicated problems here which I am sure will be dealt with at the committee stage. Therefore 1 do not intend to deal at this time with the intricacies of these matters.
In introducing the resolution I think the minister deserves the commendation of this house for the manner in which he dealt with a very intricate matter. There were facets of that resolution which could easily be misunderstood or perhaps overlooked, but the minister brought them into the foreground and I thing he explained very well the problem with which this house is confronted.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, and hoping to get the same sort of commendation now from the other side of the house, I would also say that some very good speeches generally have been made. It is given to some of us to give a fair speech, or to give a mediocre speech or to give a good speech, but once in a while it is given to some hon. members to give a great speech. I am expecting commendation now from the other side of the

Federal-Provincial Relations
house when I say that I think the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker), in which he surveyed the whole field of confederation, was a great speech which deserves the attention of the house.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I know there can be some quarrel with the arguments which he advanced. After all, he made a political speech to a political body and he is a political leader, which is all as it should be. He took the credit for having carried out certain policies, for having exercised certain authorities and for having created certain functions in which he took pride. This is of course the function of any political leader and it is one in which this party and this country also take pride.
I think he also spoke as a Canadian reviewing the whole range of confederation, taking pride in the accomplishments of the past and suggesting some of the things which he thought should be done so far as the future is concerned.
One of the suggestions or recommendations which he made was that there should be called a dominion-provincial conference, not in the technical sense of a dominion-provincial conference of the type we have had during the last few years-we have them from time to time to deal with certain specific matters-but a conference which represents all of the legislatures of the provinces and all of the political parties in Canada. It would be a conference at which, without the spotlight being focused upon it, without television or the pressure of one, two, or three days of debate, we could sit down and review the accomplishments of this country in the 97 years of its first century and look forward to the future. I think that that recommendation deserves the serious consideration of the government of the moment. There are many problems with which we are faced and they cannot be dealt with at an ad hoc conference meeting which assembles on a Tuesday afternoon, holds a dinner on the Wednesday night and another on the Thursday night, and then you say goodbye and go home on the Friday morning.
That is not the way in which confederation was accomplished. At that time the provinces were scattered and had no political connection. There was Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Upper and Lower Canada-or at that time it was the Canadas. A conference was held in 1864, another in 1865, and finally in 1867 there took place the discussions at Westminister. Out of

those conferences arose and developed a nation, Canada, of which we are all proud to be citizens.
If out of conferences of that kind, in years when the provinces were scattered and had, as I say, no direct political connection one with the other, provinces consisting largely of, shall we say, villages and hamlets and very small towns, arose this nation which we now call Canada, I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that a further conference on that basis, bringing together all the provinces and representatives of all the political parties, who in turn would represent the citizens of Canada, would surmount the problems or find solutions to the problems with which we are confronted at the moment. We all recognize, of course, that we do have problems here, but I would suggest they could be settled if this government were to consider the calling together of such a conference as suggested by the Leader of the Opposition in his speech on the resolution stage.
We have accomplished a great deal. We are considering today centennial projects which are going to cement the achievements of the last century and lay the foundations for the achievements of the next century. I suggest one approach to the solution of this problem, to which the government and this parliament should give attention, lies in the calling of a conference on the basis suggested by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker), similar to the basis upon which the conferences were called in 1864-65, and the conference in Westminster in 1867. I am quite sure if that were done a solution could be found to the problems with which we are confronted today.
Progress in this country over the last century has occurred in spite of our travels over a very rough road, and those who are pessimistic about the future of this country should look back and survey that road over which we have travelled. The development of the provinces, with scattered villages and hamlets, into a nation, represents an accomplishment by men and statesmen of all political parties working together. I am quite sure this country can be further developed, refurbished and increased in stature during the next century. As I have said, I think one of the ways by which this will take place is by calling a conference such as has been suggested by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition.
My principal purpose in rising to take part in this debate is not to discuss the details of the bill now before us. As I said earlier, I

believe the Minister of Finance has done a very good job in developing the various facets of the bill, and has given a frank, fair and full explanation of the matter. I am sure all members of this house have appreciated his endeavours in this regard. I do not intend to go into detail in respect of the bill at this moment, but intend primarily this afternoon to state my confidence in the future of this country. I do not believe that confederation is falling apart at the seams. I do not believe that this nation which has travelled so far over such rough territory, accomplishing all it has accomplished, is not now going to disintegrate, or is going to disintegrate at any time in the near future.
Perhaps my confidence in this regard is based to some extent on the history of my own province. All those individuals here who are students of Canadian political history will realize that Nova Scotia was perhaps the first province to present problems in respect of confederation, and the first province which intended to secede. Nova Scotia I believe was the first province which intended to create a state, not within a state but outside the state. I have in mind the situation in 1864, 1865 and 1867 when there was a provincial election in which every member who supported confederation was defeated. In 1867 there was a federal election as a prelude to the opening of this parliament during which 17 members of 18 ran against confederation as Liberal members. They were all elected. The lone Conservative member who was elected from Cumberland county did manage to eke out a majority of 65 or 67. He ran in support of confederation. That is the history of my province at that particular time.
Many students will know that Nova Scotia at that time was very prosperous. This situation was perhaps to some degree due to confederation, the loss of the wooden ship industry and the loss of markets as a result of the American civil war. I understand there were profits made from other sources including rum-running in the 1920's, although I have no knowledge of that whatsoever.
Nova Scotia before that time was perhaps the most prosperous part of this country, as I am sure some of my friends will admit who are now from Ontario, but which was Upper Canada at that time. Following confederation that prosperity disappeared. I do not suggest for one moment this disappearance was due entirely to confederation. The disappearance of wooden ships, with the development of steam and steel ships, together with the loss of markets due to the civil war had a great
Federal-Provincial Relations effect. The fact remains that Nova Scotia had been the most prosperous section of Canada and then became, to use the Minister of Finance's words, an unemployed or depressed area.
Naturally, blame in this regard was attached to confederation, and this became an issue. Nova Scotia had been Conservative in support of confederation, but every member who had given support was defeated at the next election, with the exception of the one who received the majority of approximately 67 votes. A government which pledged repeal of confederation was elected.
That is the history of my province. I do not intend to say anything further along this line this afternoon except to remind you that Hon. Joseph Howe travelled to London to demand repeal. I should also remind you that Sir Charles Tupper made a similar trip expressing the impossibility of repeal.
Finally some changes were made. These changes which were made at that time represented relatively minor adjustments in financial terms. The increase in subsidy to the province of Nova Scotia amounted to the price of one sheepskin per capita. A slogan was developed to the effect that Nova Scotia had been sold out for the price of a sheepskin. This slogan was perpetuated in political annals and campaigns for almost half a century. Scores of black flags were erected on July 1, Dominion day. There was a Liberal government in power for 47 years in the province of Nova Scotia because the Liberals had been opposed to confederation. The terrible Tories had been in favour of confederation. This situation existed for a very long time, as I suggest.
As a young man I was elected to the legislature of Nova Scotia and helped to bring down the 47 year regime of Liberals in the province. We in Nova Scotia know something of the talk of repeal. We can remember a premier going to London to demand repeal. Of course he did not accomplish his mission. That premier went on to become the minister of finance in the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. One of my predecessors, and a predecessor of the present Minister of Finance, won his prestige in parliament by his pledge for repeal. From 1891 to 1911 he was a very good minister of finance.
This was the situation that developed throughout the years, Mr. Speaker. As most of us are aware it has been dissipated as a result of a variety of factors, perhaps including the effect of the first world war and the

Federal-Provincial Relations efforts of Sir Robert Borden. Sir Robert Borden insisted, for instance, that Canada sign the league of nations charter as an independent nation rather than as a colony of Great Britain. That fact may have had something to do with the change of attitude. A great deal of pride gradually developed in Canada. Instead of referring in Nova Scotia to Upper and Lower Canada we began to speak as Canadians. We took pride in Canada, despite the fact that for many, many years the premiers of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, and later even the premier of Newfoundland returned from Ottawa saying they had not received a fair deal from the government of Canada.
I do not want to speak personally, Mr. Speaker, but I can remember when the premier of your province, Newfoundland, returned from here and said he was going to lead your province out of confederation because of the raw deal it had received as a province of Canada. We had the same situation with regard to the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island during those years. Nevertheless, despite the pressures, despite the criticism and despite all the problems with which we were confronted, and we were confronted with many, we did evolve a Canadian patriotism, a Canadian statemanship and a Canadian position. I think we have it today, in fact I know we have it today.
The president of a Canadian historical association-I did not have time to look up the name-made a speech about 20 years ago. There are hon. members presently in the house who know the gentleman very well. In his report to the Canadian historical association he stated that Canadians were the most introspective people in the world. He said that every morning we were inclined to take out our livers, prop them up on our knees and look at them to see if we had cirrhosis. If we did not have it, we were slightly disappointed. I think that is one of the difficulties under which we labour. We worry about Canada. We worry about confederation falling apart. We worry about all these problems with which we have lived and which we have surmounted and will continue to surmount as time passes.
I said that in the maritimes we overcame these problems. I do not want to get political about these matters, but politics does enter into them. After 1957, we did get an adjustment of our grants. We found that our coal, instead of lying in the ground, could be sold. We provided subventions for the movement

of that coal to upper Canada. We received an equalization grant, the like of which we had never received before. We had a power grid developed in the maritime provinces. We had a new outlook given to us by the government of Canada, and that government was led at that time by the right hon. gentleman who is now the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker).
I could go on and explore the various facets of this subject, particularly the Atlantic provinces adjustment grant. I think the time has come when the minister should review that grant. We provided first $25 million, and it was afterwards increased to $35 million. I think the time has come when that has to be increased still further. One could go on and on dealing with the various problems with which the government of Canada dealt between 1957 and 1963. As I have said, I think the old feeling of secession had evaporated before that. We had through war, through loyalty and through development, become Canadians rather than citizens of Nova Scotia, Upper Canada or Lower Canada. As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said, speaking on this matter a few weeks ago, he found usually when people talked about the principle of a matter they were talking about dollars and cents. I think we found in the maritime provinces that it was an adjustment in dollars and cents which went a long way toward alleviating the conditions under which we had operated. They could be alleviated still further.
We still have a lower per capita income than many other parts of Canada. We have economic problems with which we are confronted and with which the government of Canada will have to deal. There are matters of detail with which we shall have to deal when we get into the estimates later, such as the matter to which my friend the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Muir) referred this morning, namely the Atlantic provinces development board and the subsidies which should be provided through it. These are matters of pressing importance. What I want to register at the moment is that we, in the maritimes-I am speaking now as a Nova Scotian primarily-have come through an era of wanting to secede, of wanting to see this nation broken down. Today I presume there are no people more determined to see Canada maintained and developed as a nation than those who live in the Atlantic provinces.
I say therefore as I did when I started to speak, one of my purposes in speaking here today is to register my conviction that Can-

ada is not falling apart at the seams; confederation is not failing. We in the maritimes, having survived the problems with which we have been confronted, I am sure the other parts of Canada will do likewise. As I said earlier if we were to hold a conference such as the Leader of the Opposition suggested during his speech at the resolution stage, we could go ahead into the second century and develop our country even more than we have to date.
The other night the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) referred to our patching of the ship of confederation. I think we have gone about as far as we can with patching it.
I think we have to reconsider the whole basis of our confederation. I do not believe the constitution has to be scrapped. We cannot use the term "repatriation of our constitution", because we never had it here in the first place. However there are adjustments that can be made and will be made in the constitution which will make our confederation, which was established in 1867 and the centenary of which we are approaching, applicable, modern, streamlined and flexible so that this nation will continue to improve in the second century as it has in the first.
When we talk about what we have accomplished, Mr. Speaker, we only have to think of the series of little hamlets and villages scattered across several thousand miles; provinces which were not connected with other provinces and which, at least in so far as the provinces of Canada were concerned, were warring one with another, merging in order to avoid war. We had the east block and west block erected before confederation in order to accommodate these people. When you think of what we have done in 97 years, then to say that confederation is collapsing is ridiculous. We have a potential which is unequalled by any other country in the world for going ahead and developing our status as a nation.
I am not going into the economics now, but we have a unique situation. We have a privately owned railway crossing this nation, and we have a nationally owned railway crossing this nation. No other nation has that. We had until a short time ago a national system of radio and television and now we have a private system and a national system. You can go through our institutions, Mr. Speaker, and examine any one of them and you will find we have made a unique contribution to the development of a nation, one in which we should take pride instead of one for which we are apologizing. As I said, we should stop taking out our livers, propping
Federal-Provincial Relations them up on our knees and examining them to see whether or not we have cirrhosis. We should take pride in the fact we are Canadians and have developed a record of which any country in the world can be proud. I do not want to go on in this vein, Mr. Speaker.
I do not think it is necessary. I am sure there is no hon. member in this house who does not agree substantially with what I am saying today.
We are verging on the centennial of our national development and, as I said earlier, one of the things I think should be done as one of our centennial contributions is the holding of a national conference, such as was suggested by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition some time ago, and to which I referred earlier in my remarks, to lay again the foundations, as they did in 1864, 1865 and 1867. And I will assure you of one thing, Mr. Speaker, there will be no premier from Nova Scotia coming to that conference in our second century and suggesting Nova Scotia should secede.
We are of course dealing with a technical bill and I did not intend, and do not intend, to deal primarily with the technicalities of it. We will deal with those in committee. But I would say a word or two to the Minister of Finance who is here, and who has the responsibility of having control of the fiscal and financial development of Canada, or at least of the fiscal and financial measures. It is a very difficult problem with which he has to deal. There was a time when the minister of finance did have control over fiscal measures. I am not speaking of the present minister personally, or of his party personally, because this is a matter which has grown up over the years; nor am I speaking politically, although this is something which has been accelerated tremendously in the last year or two. But I am just wondering how much control the minister has over fiscal policies of this country today. I ask, is it enough? I suggest that he should maintain a relatively high degree of control over fiscal policy, but I know we all utter these cliches. I have done it. The Minister of Finance has done it, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition has done it, and everyone speaking here says, "Oh, we must have a strong federal government and we must provide for all of the legitimate demands of the provinces." That is a very easy thing to say, Mr. Speaker, but it is a very difficult matter to administer, and I am sure no one knows it better than the Minister of Finance.

I checked those this morning and, according to the figures filed by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition- official figures given to the last dominion-provincial conference, not his own figures- $1,946 million was spent by the federal government for the year ending March 1964 in assistance to and co-operation with the provinces. Leader of the Opposition produced those figures just a few short days ago.
I think we are facing a situation where the minister of finance-not speaking personally, but the minister of finance as a minister, an institution-has ceased to be a dominant factor in the fiscal policies of the country. As a matter of fact, if the present policies continue he will be a minor factor in the fiscal control of this country in the very near future. Financially, thank heaven, he does still exercise financial control over financial policies of the government. I hope that in a short while, as the house passes second reading and the committee considers this bill, we will consider the responsibility of the minister of finance, of the parliament of Canada, of the government of Canada-whoever it may be-in dealing with the fiscal and financial policies of the country.
We talk about medicare. I am sure the minister knows very well that with the hospital schemes such as we have in the various provinces a system of medicare could be mobilized. You would not have a doctor go to a house to treat a youngster for a bellyache, but you would have a degree of medicare over which the Minister of Finance would have no control whatever.
The minister has said this; I have said it and the Globe and Mail were very critical of me for saying it-that there was a very narrow area in which the Minister of Finance could operate. I repeat there is a very narrow area in which the Minister of Finance can operate today, and the area is getting narrower. We are narrowing it much more by this bill which we have before us today, which I hope will soon secure second reading. 

These, Mr. Speaker, are some of the problems, and I apologize to the house for discussing the matter at length. I know we want to get into committee and discuss the details of the bill, but I had it in mind to express myself on (a) the desirability of a conference to lay foundations for Canada for its second century; (b) my confidence in the fact that this nation is not falling asunder, falling apart and, (c) that there are problems with which the minister and the house have to deal in maintaining financial and fiscal control. I am afraid we have lost the fiscal control and, unless we watch it very carefully we may end up with loss of financial control and balkanize the nation, which our forefathers foresaw in 1864, 1865 and 1867, and which we are determined to continue now into its second century.

The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) raised a most important question, in my opinion, toward the end of his speech when he questioned the extent of the control a federal minister of finance is now in a position to exercise over the fiscal policies of the nation. It does, I suppose depend on definitions, but if fiscal policy can be expanded to include economic policy in general I should like to state my personal conviction that the federal government, including the federal minister of finance, must be in a position to influence economic policy throughout the nation in the broadest sense of that term. I believe all members of the house must take care to see that this situation continues. I have felt, as I suggest many other members have felt who are interested in this difficult problem of extracting taxes from reluctant taxpayers and deciding who would collect the taxes and who would meet the expenditures, that closer consideration should be given to the question of how much of the tax collecting and how much of the spending should be done by the federal government and how much should be done by the provinces, or by the municipalities under them.
I said the other day that I thought a good many people have been wondering-I must say I have been doing so myself-whether it would not be better, at least in some cases, if the level of government which is responsible for the administration of programs of expenditure were responsible at the same time for the collection of the taxes needed to pay for those programs. I would at once qualify what I have said by adding that I am one of those who believe implicitly in the principle

Federal-Provincial Relations of equalization, because if there were not some principle of equalization so that moneys which happen to be collected in certain parts of Canada could be spread fairly throughout the country, then we would have nothing like equal standards of services throughout Canada, and in those circumstances I can well believe questions would arise as to the desirability of holding this country together. Let us make no mistake about it, it is important that we do the things which are necessary to maintain a reasonably fair standard of services throughout Canada.
I suppose I had the same concern as the hon. gentleman experienced when he took over the portfolio which I have the honour to hold at the moment, about the extent to which the federal government or the federal minister of finance can influence the various aspects of economic policy. One of the important areas, and one which probably should not be mentioned at this particular moment, is the area of monetary policy and the influence which monetary policy in other countries now has on the flexibility we have in Canada. The hon. gentleman questioned whether the federal minister of finance now plays a dominant role in the formulation of fiscal and, I would add, economic policies in Canada. I would like to say that if I believed that the federal minister of finance was not able to play the most important role in those areas-I would not say the sole role, by any means-then I, for one, would have no wish to continue as federal minister of finance. I do not believe for one moment that the federal minister of finance or the federal government, which I think is the better way of putting it, has lost that dominant influence. There will always be a struggle or difference of opinion in any federal state as to the extent to which the federal and provincial governments respectively should control policy, but I am one of those who think that greater discussion between the people responsible for policy in these areas at the federal and provincial levels is highly desirable. The government is hopeful that the proposed tax structure committee, which will be set up by the federal and provincial governments together will over a period of years try to iron out some of the obvious ambiguities or anomalies in our present division of taxes and also, I would hope, in the present division of responsibilities for various areas of policy.
I am also hopeful that the proposal that the finance or economic ministers of the federal and provincial governments should 

meet annually in the late fall will be something that will be productive and useful. It seems to me that if this gets started on the right note and if we recognize that collectively we have a responsibility that transcends party politics we can do something in this area. I hope it will be successful or at least that it will be helpful, although I think we must recognize that there will always be tugs and pulls between the federal and the provincial governments.
I was very pleased to hear the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) say, if I interpreted him correctly, that he was heartily in favour of the system of federal-provincial fiscal relations that has evolved, even though he felt it proper and desirable to criticize some aspects of the formula that has been developed. He suggested, if I interpreted him correctly, that the proposals contained in the bill represented some improvement but he is still not satisfied. Like him, I hope we will never be satisfied that we have reached perfection in this or any other field.
The hon. member questioned in particular, if I recall correctly, the basis of the equalization formula and raised the question why resource revenues should be taken into account to some extent in arriving at equalization and why the additional 25 per cent abatement in the estate tax that was agreed to last November is not subject to equalization. The first question he asked was: To what extent has the Bank of Canada purchased government bonds? Might I say in reply that as at June 30, 1964 the Bank of Canada owned a total of $2,925 million government of Canada direct and guaranteed securities, the breakdown being as follows: treasury bills, $403.3 million; bonds of two years and under, $389.6 million; bonds of over two years to five years, $549.1 million; over five to ten years, $874.9 million; and over ten years, $708.2 million. This makes a grand total of $2,925 million. These holdings comprise 14.6 per cent of the total government securities outstanding at June 30, 1964.
The second question was: What is the average length of time that these bonds are likely to be held until they do mature or before they are sold? The answer is that the Bank of Canada in the course of its open market operations buys and sells government of Canada securities. Decisions as to the over-all direction of these operations and the particular securities which are bought and sold are made within the context of the monetary policy being carried out by the Bank of Canada, with the approval of the government. It would be impossible to make a general statement as to the length of time the securities have been held in the past or will be held in the future. I think the table I have given does give some idea of the breakdown of the Bank of Canada's holdings at that particular time.
The third question was: How much money is actually paid to the Bank of Canada in interest on these bonds which the Bank of Canada holds? What portion of these charges is returned, this accruement of interest charges on government bonds held by the Bank of Canada, to the consolidated revenue fund? In reply I would point out that the Bank of Canada pays over the surplus available from its operations to the consoli-


dated revenue fund every year. In 1963 the income of the bank from investments, which included income from interest on bonds and treasury bills, totalled $127,407,000. The total income of the bank was $127,851,000, and the net income paid to the consolidated revenue fund was $116,386,000. So it is quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that with the exception of operating costs and that sort of thing all of the interest which is paid to the Bank of Canada is paid back again in the form of profits to the consolidated revenue fund.
There is one other point on which I would ask the house to bear with me if I reply to it in detail. It is in connection with the figures which were read into the record last night by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Grer goire). He referred to some figures which were supplied by Mr. K. W. Taylor when he was deputy minister of finance early in 1963 to Mr. Maurice Allard, the former member for Sherbrooke. Mr. Allard has given these figures wide currency in the province of Quebec and I feel it is desirable that we take note of them and of their serious deficiencies, and also of the misleading conclusions which have been drawn from them. Several hon. members have asked questions on these matters, which have been made orders for returns, and the Department of Finance has been working for some months to try and get together some material which would produce a reasonable answer to the questions which have been asked. This is a matter which has proven to be of great complexity and difficulty, and I should like to refer to this in connection with the figures put on the record by the hon. member.
First of all, I should like to read to hon. members the English version of the letter sent to Mr. Allard, and I should be happy to table a copy of the letter which was actually sent in French, so that hon. members may see for themselves that there is no problem arising from the translation. The following is the English version from which the French was produced. The letter is dated February 4, 1963 and reads:
Dear Mr. Allard,
I have been asked by Mr. Heward Grafftey, M.P.r parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance, to reply to your letter of January 24, 1963, in which you ask what revenues were received from, and what payments were made to, the province of Quebec by the federal government in 1961.
In answer to your question I wish to advise that during the fiscal year ended March 31, 1961 revenues collected by the federal government in the province of Quebec were estimated to be $1,748.9 million while payments to the province were estimated as $1,072.7 million. It must be noted, however,

that the following qualifications apply to the compilation of the above amounts:-
And it is these qualifications which sometimes are not noted with too much emphasis in some of the speeches which we hear.
(a)	Corporation taxes paid by the head offices in the province of Quebec are not allocated to the other provinces.
That in itself throws these figures completely out of kilter and in my opinion makes them utterly misleading.
(b)	Revenues of the customs and excise division included in gross amount as refunds are not allocated to individual provinces; also, the port of Montreal collects considerable amounts in customs duties that properly apply to other provinces but which do not lend themselves to allocation. Similarly, certain collections made by the Ottawa district taxation office apply to the counties of Hull, Gatineau and Pontiac.
(c)	The expenditure figure does not include:
(i)	The more general type of budgetary expenditures which are made for the benefit of the country as a whole and of direct benefit to all provinces. In this category are the expenses of the central legislative body at Ottawa, financial and administrative departments at Ottawa, the foreign service and the research activities of the national research council.
(ii)	Payments to a number of suppliers of goods and services as the payments in many cases are made to the head offices of the companies and therefore do not lend themselves to accurate allocation by provinces.
(iii)	Operations of the post office as the expenditures are considered to more or less offset the revenues collected by that department.
(iv)	Payments to the national conference of Canadian universities.
Yours sincerely,
K. W. Taylor.
It will be seen from this that the qualifications which Mr. Taylor carefully applied to these figures are most important and material.
I apologize again for taking time to make this point, but I should ask for permission to carry on for a few moments as I think it is important that the facts of this matter are put on the record so that my hon. friends, unwittingly I am sure, will not again use the earlier material which has been very misleading in many parts of the country.
Much of the corporation taxes paid by head offices in the province of Quebec are properly allocated to other provinces, as we do under our fiscal arrangements. The customs collected in the ports of Montreal are really paid by people in many parts of Canada, and do not in fact represent revenues collected from the people or province of Quebec even though they are collected in the ports in the province. I have no doubt that the same point would apply to a good deal of the federal sales
Federal-Provincial Relations taxes collected from manufacturers in the province of Quebec on products sold to buyers in other provinces. It will also be noted that the expenditure figures do not include a number of categories, as well.
The Ontario figures which the hon. member quoted are subject to the same qualifications and exhibit the same kind of differences. It is perfectly evident that during this time, as at the present, the federal government is paying out as much as it takes in, one way or another, and it is not withholding the huge amounts that these figures are interpreted to suggest. In fact the federal government is paying out more than it takes in, if I remember correctly.

The Department of Finance has endeavoured to allocate fairly as much as it could of the federal revenues, by provinces, for the year 1961-62. This endeavour has been taking place over the last several months. I may say the departmental officials have been struggling with this problem for quite some time. They reviewed the situation with me early this week, and it is obvious that these calculations involve so many assumptions, so many ifs, ands and buts, that as a one-time accountant I was pretty nervous about them.
It is possible to make this kind of calculation in respect of individual and corporate income tax, estate tax, and as a result of some detailed studies, for taxes on alcoholic beverages, tobacco and related products. These revenues that can be allocated in this way amounted to a total of some $4,163 million. The balance of approximately $2,184 million of federal revenue cannot be allocated properly by province. That balance represents something over one third of federal revenue. This total figure which I have mentioned does not include amounts collected under tax rental agreements, but it does include amounts collected for old age security and unemployment insurance, as well as certain smaller items. It is evident from these figures that it is not possible to get an allocation of total revenues which can be compared with expenditures made to people in the various provinces or for their benefit.
The Department of Finance has made a detailed study of the expenditures and finds it can allocate approximately 40 per cent of gross federal expenditures to provinces by residence of recipient. This includes social security payments made directly to individuals, and various payments made to provincial governments and provincial institutions. Another 16 per cent of our expenditures can be roughly allocated by provinces on the basis of the location of the works on which they are spent or the service which they are used to provide. When these are eliminated this leaves about 44 per cent of the gross expenditures for items which cannot be said to be paid for the benefit of people in any particular province, and these can only be distributed arbitrarily, for example,


on the basis of population. This would not include, for example, expenditures on parliament itself and the various central services of the government, expenses incurred in public debt charges, in external affairs and in national defence. It also includes various expenditures on research and a variety of other general services provided by the federal government on a national basis.
The expenditures, which we have endeavoured to study and allocate in this way, amounted-and this refers to the whole 100 per cent-to approximately $7,246 million in 1961-62.
In view of what I have said, I do not think that any meaningful comparisons can be drawn between the expenditures which we can allocate to persons in a particular province and revenues we can allocate as being collected from persons in a particular province, unless we make arbitrary assumptions as to how these can be assumed to affect persons, provincial institutions and governments indirectly.
Time has only permitted the department to make a detailed study of this nature for the year 1961-62. We shall provide the details of these figures in answer to the questions to which I have referred. I thought, however, that at this point in this debate I should make clear the general nature and content of the figures, and to say that they show that the statements made on the basis of the letter, to which the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) made reference, and which I have read into the record, are misleading and based on information that is inevitably incomplete.

I commend it also to some of the editorial writers who ought to study it with considerable reflection.
On July 7 the right hon. Leader of the Opposition put forward a proposal for a full-fledged dominion-provincial conference on matters dealing with fiscal relations, national symbols and other matters such as the patria-tion of our constitution; all those things which go toward national unity. I saw some criticisms of this suggestion the following day, and I thought they were most ill-considered.
Federal-Provincial Relations I do not believe the writers had really seen the text of what the right hon. gentleman had said. I am sure the minister does realize that there is a terrible problem existing in this country in connection with priorities of expenditures on education, health and welfare. These problems have grown within the past five years or possibly ten years, and have become much more acute. About five years ago we were not spending a great deal of money from the federal point of view on hospital insurance. Around the corner is the proposal for medicare. What the expenditure is likely to be for that-

We are caught in this horrible dilemma because of a lack of agreement on priorities. We are getting pressure from the various provinces to opt out of this or that program, and opting out is a phrase coined by my hon. friends opposite. It is not limited to the province of Quebec. We have even heard it said in Alberta that so far as hospital and diagnostic services are concerned, if they could have the revenues they would like to run the show themselves. It is a more immediate step, and is necessary because I feel that with this growing participation in joint programs, in the fiscal relations between provinces and the federal government we must do away with this principle of opting out, and we must do as much as possible to eliminate the conditions that lead to it.
If the provinces agreed, education should have a certain priority, health should have a priority and welfare a priority. Then there

Sometimes I am a little short tempered at this insistence on the rights of provinces. It is always the rights of the provinces and, dealing with education, we know this is in the constitution, but I would like to see a better look taken at the responsibilities with respect to education.

Federal-Provincial Relations one province and allocate to that particular province certain moneys, and then draw conclusions from that. I think there is nothing more misleading than this type of consideration. To say that Ontario, or Quebec, pay into the federal treasury far more money than they get out of it leads to an illogical position. The same is true with regard to any other province. I do not know whether this is Social Credit policy or not, I hear a great many such statements made out in Alberta, too. There are provincial cabinet ministers and members of the legislature who say that Alberta pays so much into the federal treasury and only gets so much back. This leaves out a great deal. For instance, the income tax paid by the head offices of our chartered banks comes mainly out of two provinces, yet the earnings are derived from provinces all over Canada. Consider the situation of the major oil companies. British American Oil and Imperial Oil do not pay their income tax out of offices in Edmonton or Calgary but out of Toronto or Montreal. The Canadian Pacific Railway is another example. This division of provincial revenue on the basis of funds contributed and received becomes nonsensical.
In addition, we could talk about defence. Those who live in the maritimes or in the western provinces could say: What about all the defence spending done by the Department of Defence Production in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec? Does that not constitute a return to those provinces to the extent of this defence expenditure? Nothing is said about that.
Any conclusion reached as to these revenues must be so conditional that it can no longer be regarded as valid. All one can say is that the federal government collects so much money and spends so much money. I do not know how anything else can be said. What about the excise tax on the distillation of spirit alcohol, for instance, which emanates mainly from Ontario and Quebec? This is a most important fiscal consideration. I do not believe for a moment that the people of Ontario and Quebec have a monopoly on the consumption of these spirit liquors. These spirits are drunk from one end of the country to another and the tax is paid by the people in the provinces where the liquor is consumed. The same applies to tobacco. So let us forget all about trying to allocate revenues and expenditures within provinces, because doing so does not lead to any meaningful conclusions.

I am not sure I can completely support his approval of the suggestion made by the premier of Manitoba. I have a high regard for the ability of the premier of Manitoba and I think any suggestions he has to make should be considered very seriously. Nevertheless, I am not at all sure that it would be desirable to hold a conference on priorities confined within the framework of education, hospitalization, welfare and medical services. If these matters were considered outside the context of the general economic state of the nation and the general policies which might be formulated with regard to fiscal relations between the provincial governments and the federal governments, such a conference might tend to produce a false impression of what the priorities really are. It might, for instance, suggest that what we needed was more education and less health care, or vice-versa, whereas on the basis of the over-all situation in the country with regard to priorities, in my view at least we should be making progress rapidly in both those fields.
However, I wish primarily to raise some questions in respect of two particular points concerning the formula which have already been dealt with by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, namely the non-inclusion of the additional 25 per cent rebate on estate tax and the newly devised policy of taking into account natural resource revenues within the provinces. When the minister was concluding the debate on second reading I was quite pleased to note that he indicated his agreement with the belief of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in the principle of equalization, as far as the distribution of revenues from the shared tax fields is concerned. I was not surprised that in this connection the Minister of Finance is in agreement with statements that have been made by the present Prime Minister of Canada. In this regard I should like to refer briefly to the statement made by the then premier of Saskatchewan at the federal-provincial conference in November of last

year in which he quoted with approval an earlier statement made by the present Prime Minister. In his opening statement to the conference the then premier of Saskatchewan had this to say, as found on page 93 of the report:
What I mean is the concept which the Prime Minister so clearly stated in 1958.
Then he quotes the Prime Minister as follows:
All provinces should receive an equal revenue per head of population from the tax field shared between the two levels of government.
What concerns me, and I have not heard any explanation yet from the Minister of Finance, is why, when he says he believes in the principle of equalization and when the present Prime Minister has on previous occasions stated so clearly his belief in the principle of equalization, in the particular formula proposed in the bill the minister has so clearly departed from the principle of equalization in respect of the increased rebate of estate taxes. In answer to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam all that the Minister of Finance has said so far is: We are going to do it. But he has not told us why. Nor has he made any attempt as far as I can determine to relate the reasons for doing so to his avowed belief in the principle of equalization. Nor has he, as far as I was able to determine from listening to him, given us any rational explanation of why at this time he is asking us to agree to an exception to this principle.
Before we proceed too much farther with the discussion in committee and the passage of the bill, I think the minister should explain in greater detail than he has so far why he is agreeing to this being done. If he does not do so, we are going to have to try to work out some kind of theory as to why he has done this, and we may not come up with the right conclusion. We may branch off into speculation that is completely off the track as to the reason for this action.
I should like to give an example of the direction in which speculation may very well turn. I believe I am correct in saying that in answer to questions at the resolution stage with regard to what had taken place at the federal-provincial conference the minister made a statement to the effect that the premier of British Columbia had indicated he was very happy with the idea of excluding the additional 25 per cent from the equalization formula.

Federal-Provincial Relations
exclusion from the formula of the 25 per cent increase in the rebate.
As one who believes in the principle of equalization, I would say that if there is any one of the three tax fields which should be equalized more than any other it is the estate tax field, because of the fact that there tend to be concentrations of wealth in certain centres which are accumulated from all across the country. When the minister was closing the debate on second reading and discussing the figures presented by the hon. member for Lapointe, I think he brought out that situation very well. I should like the minister to enlighten us further on this question.
While on this subject I also want to make it very clear that although it is true that at the federal-provincial conferences the premier of British Columbia speaks for the government of British Columbia, which purports to speak for the people of British Columbia- he certainly speaks as expressing the policies which are going to be put into effect in the province-there are a great many of us in British Columbia who could not differ more diametrically from the attitude expressed by the premier of British Columbia at the federal-provincial conference last November. In his statements he is doing what he so often does; he is attempting to distort the constitution of this country in an effort, in my view, to get his own way, thereby creating unnecessary tensions in confederation. I made the statement that the premier of British Columbia is the greatest separatist in Canada; I used the phrase that he could "out-Caouette Caouette". If he was sitting in this house I am sure that his only spiritual home would be a seat close to the hon. member for Lapointe.
The premier of British Columbia has been saying a great deal lately about his belief in co-operative federalism, but when one reads the fine print contained in the kind of proposals he puts before a federal-provincial conference, then I think it is not unfair to say that by his attitude he is perhaps the greatest separatist in the country today. As one citizen of British Columbia I want to make it clear to the Minister of Finance that this is an attitude and a frame of mind with which I thoroughly disagree.
I was quite interested in the remarks made earlier by the hon. member for Digby-Annap-olis-Kings to the effect that it was long ago that the people of Nova Scotia forgot about the kind of outlook which is now advocated


by the present premier of the province from which I come.
Having said that, I should like to move on to the second question concerning the business of including in the formula a provision for taking into account natural resources revenue. A great deal has already been said on this subject by members from the province of British Columbia, and I for one agree with the serious questions which have been raised by other members from British Columbia as to the desirability and the reasonableness of taking into account this particular element of the formula.
It might be argued that it is a relatively academic question as far as British Columbia is concerned because it really does not affect the balance of payments to British Columbia by that much, as matters stand at the moment. At least that is the way I interpret the figure. However, to me it does raise some serious question as to whether it is an equitable and desirable principle to incorporate in arrangements regarding equalization for distribution of taxes. It seems to me that the question of the revenue which a province draws into its provincial treasury from natural resources is not necessarily related in any way to the natural wealth or natural resources of the province, but rather to the policies which a particular provincial government may have seen fit to implement with respect to levies which are made and which draw revenue to the provincial government from those resources. It may be that one province levies a realistic charge, for example, on those who harvest the forest crops. Another province may practically give them away, at least as far as any direct revenue to the provincial treasury is concerned, and therefore would have no revenue.
Several hon. members have already mentioned the question of what is gross revenue and what is net revenue in this regard. As far as British Columbia is concerned-I realize this is a matter which has to be discussed in detail in another forum than this one-a great many of us have felt that over the years the policy of British Columbia governments has been faulty on two counts. One is that they have not drawn into the provincial treasury sufficient revenues from our basic natural resources, forest resources in particular. Up until comparatively recent years they have been the main source of natural resource revenue, although as we all know gas and oil has become an increasingly important element in the natural resource picture in British Columbia. On the second

count, an insufficient portion of the natural resources revenue is being reinvested or ploughed back into the development and perpetuation of those resources, again with particular reference to forest resources.
Earlier in the discussion of this measure reference was made to this matter by the hon. member for Cariboo, who of course also comes from the province of British Columbia but as everyone realizes is in a slightly different part of the political spectrum of the province. He made some reference to the amount that it costs the province of British Columbia to construct access roads, the cost of reforestation, fire protection, and so on, and he suggested that this was a rather expensive process.
I have before me a copy of the public accounts for the province of British Columbia for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1964, and as far as I can understand the figures they do bear out the fact that there is a fairly substantial revenue now coming in from the natural resources field, but that really the portion which is being ploughed back into the resources field is not very substantial in comparison with the total. I have taken the figure for the total revenue from natural resources during the last fiscal year to be $75,804,000 and the total expenditures to be $22,180,000, which leaves a balance of provincial funds over and above expenditure of $53,623,000, which means that less than one third of what is taken in is being spent on the development of such things as fire protection, reforestation, forest access roads and the like. I would not want to say that I have taken into account every factor which may be involved in those figures. The total expenditure figures which I have quoted are taken from the expenditures of the departments of lands and forests, recreation, conservation and mines. Also there may be certain other expenditures of a more minor nature which I have not included.
The point I am trying to make is that under the formula proposed by this bill no provision is made, as far as I can understand it, apart from what I said earlier about the scale of charges which may be levied by a province, for the scale of expenditure which a province may be making for the preservation, conservation and development of these natural resources. In other words, as far as the province of British Columbia is concerned the application of this formula would make no difference; if instead of spending $22 million on resources, conservation and development, the province was spending $122 million. It
Federal-Provincial Relations could be spending half as much again as it was taking in in gross revenue, and this would still not be an element which would be used in deciding their eligibility under the equalization formula.
The minister here again, as far as I have heard so far, has explained to the committee that this is what has been done. An announcement was made in this regard by the Prime Minister at the time of the federal-provincial conference. The minister has not explained why this is being done. If one believes, as I think the minister himself has said, in the principle of equalization, one certainly should be able to expect the minister when he asks us to depart from these principles, to give us a good account of his reason, particularly when he is asking us to approve this suggestion.
While there are many of us who are prepared to do battle wherever necessary with those who oppose the principle, as does the premier of British Columbia, if we are going to be a party to the approval of a bill which is not on all fours with the principle, we find ourselves in a position of having weakened the case we represent.
Very often in British Columbia we hear the argument, one which has been suggested here in the house, that the big greedy Ottawa government is taking much more out of the province than it is putting back in. On the surface very often this argument is convincing. It is difficult for those of us who. believe in the Canadian nation to answer it. One of the best methods of coping with this argument would lie in an ability to go back to our constituencies and say that the parliament of Canada is passing arrangements in respect of federal-provincial fiscal arrangements involving redistribution in tax fields on all fours with the principle of providing an equal opportunity to Canadians in all parts of Canada. However when we must go back and say that parliament has done this only to a point, it is not very satisfactory.
Using British Columbia as an example I think will best explain my feeling, particularly now that British Columbia is going to establish its own bank and will become one of the financial centres of Canada, with increased wealth accumulations and large estates. We could perhaps say in these circumstances that we are going to hold on to this nice little pie, and keep it for ourselves, ignoring some of the other provinces which have not been able to accomplish these things.
Mr. Chairman, I hope while we are on clause 1, or when we are dealing with par



Federal-Provincial Relations ticular clauses of this bill which refer to the points I have touched on, the Minister of Finance will elucidate to a somewhat further extent than he has done so far in respect of the principles he is asking us to approve.
