speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer briefly to what the minister said in reply to the many questions which were raised before the conclusion of second reading. Unfortunately I was not present at the opening of his remarks. I came as quickly as possible, as soon as I knew he was replying.
I should like to thank him very much for expressing concern about and appreciation of some of the points I raised in my speech yesterday. I should also like to say to him that while I appreciate his concern, and thank him for his felicitations, what I really wanted was money. I did not hear him say anything about amending portions of Bill No. C-lll to take care of some of the inequities I pointed out yesterday. He said there could have been, or is, an honest difference of opinion in respect of his position and the contention I outlined regarding hospitalization cost sharing arrangements. Although I did not hear him, I think perhaps he intimated that this was also true as far as natural resource revenues are concerned, when considering these figures in light of equalization grants.
The minister said one other thing, Mr. Chairman, and I do not wish to misquote or misconstrue what he said. I believe he said there was an honest and sincere desire on the part of the federal government to meet frequently with the provinces-I think perhaps he said annually-in an attempt to work out ground rules and principles that could be applied to distribution of tax money, and that when such a set of rules and principles had been worked out all of the provinces would be treated fairly and equally within this scope. Mr. Chairman, I certainly hope that he meant what he said. If there is a disposition on the part of the federal government now to work out some kind of rules and principles so that every province of this country can share in the distribution of tax revenues on an equal basis and every citizen in this country will then be treated equally, I think that would be a step in the right direction. I hope this situation will materialize.
Mr. Chairman, in the event the minister has forgotten the position of Alberta in this respect I should like to make that position abundantly clear. The premier of the province of Alberta had the following to say in this regard:


In arriving at any new arrangement in the field of federal-provincial relations, are the specific constitutional responsibilities assigned to the respective governments, under the British North America Act, going to he respected?
Mr. Chairman, we are being told that so far as the federal government is concerned, the major reason for the amendment in Bill No. C-lll is an attempt to help the provinces take care of their responsibilities in the field of education. If it has now become a major responsibility of the federal government to help the provinces financially in the field of education, then surely we have the right to expect that this at least ought to be provided for in the constitution of Canada. In the event that some hon. members from the province of Quebec feel they are alone in demanding that the terms and conditions of the British North America Act be adhered to, I should like to point out to them that the premier of the province of Alberta has stated this:
The government of Alberta maintains they should be, not merely in theory but in fact. We are deeply concerned by the extent to which these constitutional provisions have been progressively eroded away in recent years by federal policies and programs advanced in the name of the national public interest. We do not accept the premise that it is necessary to violate the constitution in order to meet any alleged national need. We believe in every case there is a more desirable alternate way of meeting such needs without violating either the letter or the spirit of the B.N.A. Act. We desire to have this matter clarified.
It is quite obvious, Mr. Chairman, that there are other provinces in addition to Quebec that are deeply concerned about this business of continually providing temporary expedients to meet some political promise that might have been made.
The only other thing about which I wish to comment at this time, Mr. Chairman, is this matter of priorities. The premier of Manitoba has made it clear to the federal government on a number of occasions, and again at Jasper during the past few days, that the premiers of all the provinces would like to see the federal and provincial governments sit down together to work out some list of priorities so that each level of government knows where it is going, in harmony with the other. There have been occasions on which the federal government has gone to the Canadian people during an election campaign and made certain promises. These political parties, whether Liberal or Conservative, did not consult with the provincial governments to ascertain whether or not the provinces were willing to expand social services in those areas. Then, regardless of which party was elected, it was found that in

order to fulfil those promises made in the election campaign it was necessary to impose some additional expenses on the provinces. We have seen such situations during the last few years, Mr. Chairman. There have been serious intrusions into the field of provincial administration when the federal government has passed certain measures calling upon the provincial treasuries to meet, in part, some of the expenditures to give effect to those measures.
There was an example of this situation last fall when the federal government passed a measure to increase old age assistance allowances. This required expenditure from the provincial treasury. Many of these provincial legislatures had completed their sittings at that time and had not provided in their budgets for these additional expenditures. There is, therefore, a very real need for the two levels of government to get together and agree on a set of priorities so that they can move forward in harmony when such agreement is reached. The premier of Alberta also agrees with this when he says:
In those areas where rights and responsibilities are assigned jointly to both the federal and provincial governments, what role properly should be played by each of the two levels of government?
This requires an analysis and reassessment of revenue sources and taxation policies and a review of the whole field of social welfare programs, including hospital and medical services and pensions and also other fields, such as education, Indian affairs, resources, management and development and agriculture.
It could not be made much clearer, Mr. Chairman, that the government of Alberta and the government of Manitoba would like to know in advance what the federal government intends to do by way of expanding social service programs so that they can make provision for these expansions.
I do not want to pursue this matter further at this point, Mr. Chairman. I feel it is important that the federal government is now prepared to sit down with the provinces and work out a set of principles or ground rules that will be applicable to all the provinces equally, and equitable or fair to the population of the country. This is certainly a step in the right direction and I commend the minister for the suggestion this is now the attitude of the federal government.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to speak at length on clause 1 of this bill, but I simply want to follow up a few remarks heard with regard to the statistics 1 quoted yesterday in the house.

Anyway, one thing must be kept in mind: the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) stated that he would supply us with true figures and he advanced some arguments which I cannot remember, because I think they are wrong. The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Cho-quette) tried to prove that the figures supplied by the hon. member for Lapointe were not correct, that he knew nothing about them and that the Minister of Finance would let us have his figures later. That was the basis of his argument.
We cannot accept-though maybe he can- the fact that the minister should describe those figures as false, or rather saying that, in spite of the figures supplied in Mr. Taylor's letter being correct, one and the other thing should be considered and that, as far as the
6564	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Relations actual figures were concerned, he would supply them later. He did not explicitly prove that our figures were wrong. He simply stated that he would give other figures later and that the officials of the department were analysing the things the Minister of Finance wants to take into consideration.
The Minister of Finance stated that two of those amounts were spent all across the country and that he could not show they were spent in such and such a province but rather in the general interest of the country as a whole. That we recognized yesterday when we mentioned that the government, in 1961, had collected $5,700 million in the various provinces, while it had spent $1,200 million less. It is precisely those sums of money which are not spent in any specific province but for the country as a whole that we want to know about. I gave exactly the same examples that the Minister of Finance gave, for instance, the administration of the House of Commons, the interest on the national debt. The minister used the same examples I did. The Minister of Finance said that there are amounts of money which are collected in the provinces but which cannot be said to come from a specific province. For instance, the sales tax or customs duties; and the Minister of Finance gave as an example the Montreal harbour, where goods enter from abroad and where customs duties are collected, and then the goods are shipped to other provinces. On the other hand, we must not forget that there are also the Halifax, Toronto and Vancouver harbours and that, in those harbours as well, goods enter on which customs duties are collected, and then those goods are shipped to other provinces.
If one wants-as the minister intends to do-to find out exactly what comes from a specific province, then the minister will realize that figures will not change much. That is why I would ask the Minister of Finance, before saying that we are wrong, to check the figures. We are ready to wait before making new statements, but let the Minister of Finance give us the true figures, as he promised to do, instead of saying that our figures are false and claiming that we did not want to understand the explanations. We are ready to wait for those figures, but he should first give them to us.
Yesterday I quoted figures and the Minister of Finance rose at once to say that they were false. Let him produce his figures, and then we will compare them with those supplied by Mr. Taylor, which do not take into account


the income tax on the profits of corporations whose head office is in Montreal. The same applies to corporations whose head offices are in Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver or Halifax. When trying to establish the origin of those federal sources of income, one realizes that, in any province, everything comes out even in the end.
Besides, it is just as normal for a company such as the Aluminum Company of Arvida, whose plant is located in the riding of Ville-neuve while the head office is in Montreal, to pay taxes to the province of Quebec and sell goods in Ontario and in western provinces, as it is for a company whose plant is in the United States, to pay taxes to the American government and then sell its goods in foreign countries. Such a thing normally exists between different countries and it exists also between the various provinces. Every province has its own taxes; every province collects its own taxes.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I merely wanted to make this quite clear, before the Minister of Finance or the hon. member for Lotbiniere or the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) or the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) or others contend that our figures are wrong. They should start by giving us their own figures and until then, they should stop saying that the hon. member for Lapointe is in error.
Let them not say; "The hon. member for Lapointe is mistaken; we will give figures in two months' time." No. We are willing to wait until they give their figures. They should show the same goodwill as we do and let us see their figures; we would then be in a better position to discuss the issues.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the point I wanted to clear up. The Minister of Finance stated he was ready to put other statistical data on the record, and we are quite willing to wait. In the meantime, however, he should be as courteous to us as we were to him and he should not question our figures. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that anyone who has heard some of the remarks made in this chamber today, indeed anyone who has over the last few years noticed the amount of stress and strain between the dominion and the provinces will realize that really what we have been doing from time to time is quite a patchwork of trying to satisfy the growing needs of various provinces, as their responsibilities grow heavier on them.

I think it is time we took a look, not just at the fiscal arrangements but at the duties and responsibilities of the governments themselves. In my opinion the B.N.A. Act is a little out of date. I believe that the responsibilities of the federal government might be eased somewhat by giving more responsibilities to provinces, and I think if we were now to align in a sensible manner some of the duties and responsibilities of the provinces, we could transfer some of their duties to the federal government.
I cannot see how any long term arrangement can be worked out that will get us out of this ever recurring struggle to make another concession here or grant another small amount of money there. The trouble with most of us in this chamber is that we have not looked closely enough at the changing conditions in the world today, at the demands made on the federal government in the context of a new modern world. Certainly ever since people have begun to be better educated, ever since we have begun to realize the extent to which automation and new methods of production could make ever higher standards of living available, it has been obvious that our demands for more and more of the better things of life have been increasing even faster than the methods of production can provide them. This has brought about, not just in Canada but in all other countries, a greater intervention of government in business.
I know there are those who believe in private enterprise who used to say a few years ago that it was the business of government to create an economic atmosphere in which private enterprise could flourish, but I believe we have left that concept far behind. The idea has been accepted and acted upon, not only in this country but in others, and not only in the federal government but in the provincial governments, that there are areas and fields in which only the provincial governments or the federal government have the authority and the means, and only government itself can control the factors which will aid private enterprise.
To give just one slight example, there is the roads to resources program. We can all concede that while there might be some very valuable timber that any efficient private enterprise could get out and could profitably sell in this country and abroad, sometimes the accessibility of that timber involves dredging a new canal, building a new railroad or providing new roads, all of these projects being out of the reach of practical financing by 20220-415J
Federal-Provincial Relations most companies. I am aware that in some places, for example where there are vast iron mine resources, very large corporations with very huge sums behind them have been able to get together and build very substantial railroads and docks, and provide the ships and all the rest; but as a general rule undertakings of this nature require concessions by government that are few and far between; and there are many other pools of resources where provincial governments find that properly directed public funds can open up an area where private enterprise can exploit the resources and healthy competition can exist.
I have previously made reference in this chamber to the difference today as compared with a few years ago in international trade circles. Most of us are aware that there are state trading nations, such as the communist countries, where it is the government itself which does the trading, where our manufacturers who do business on a private industry basis have to compete with the entire weight and influence of foreign nations when they are seeking foreign markets. Even countries such as Japan, which rely on state trading cartels, are a little too much competition for individual exporters from this country in world markets.
While many of us in this house value local autonomy and have great respect for provincial rights, when we reflect on the conditions which exist in the world today we are bound to concede that the power of the federal government must remain very strong. In fact in many fields, especially in the field of commerce, this strength must be increased if we are to hold our own successfully with other countries. If our private traders are unable to compete without government assistance of some kind or another, then we can no longer remain in the forefront of the nations of the world today, with our high standard of living.
It is axiomatic, I think, that the government can only carry out those projects which it is able to finance, and I submit that the major responsibility for keeping Canada an important country in the world today can only be assumed at the federal level. If we are not to have interprovincial conflicts to an extent which might seriously weaken the country as a whole, I suggest that every Canadian should have an equal opportunity, that the provinces should review the rights which have been entrusted to them and that the question of how much money should be made

Federal-Provincial Relations available to each province should be resolved as fairly as possible.
The hon. member for Peace River made a reference in this house recently to the steps being taken in the province of Quebec to encourage industry to settle there. Certainly it is logical that any provincial government should try to encourage industry to come to its own province. I know that the federal government has taken the initiative from time to time in designating areas where the economic growth is so much less than it might be that it is thought necessary for the central authority to try to encourage industry to locate there. But when there is too much incentive given to industry to locate in one particular province rather than in another, we find ourselves confronted with the equivalent of trade barriers erected between the provinces. I believe we must strive to place as much emphasis as we can on getting industry to come to Canada. The question of the location of industry within one province or another should relate entirely to those natural economic factors which give industry an advantage-efficient means of communication, a pool of labour, the natural resources upon which it is relying, and so on. Certainly if because of the zealousness of particular provinces-the fact, for instance, that the tax structure has been made to offer highly artificial advantages-industry finds that it is advantageous to locate in one province rather than in another, it may be that since, the enterprise has failed to take advantage of the factors which would naturally lead to its efficiency, it is unable to sell its product successfully on world markets, with the result that all Canada is poorer.
I realize a suggestion that there should be a limitation placed on the extent to which provinces could discriminate in favour of industry in this way is bound to be the subject of heated debate. I am not yet clear in my own mind whether it would be better to have uniformity of legislation agreed on between the provinces in this respect or whether it would be desirable to remove from the provinces some of their power to penalize or reward companies for locating in one area rather than in another. I know there are companies who are studying this situation very seriously. Many companies have to make up their minds whether they will make a serious effort to get into the export market or whether they will simply concentrate on trading within Canada. Once we get to this stage, I think all of us are concerned, first of all, for the good of Canada. If Canada cannot

remain strong and healthy in the field of international trade, each of the provinces will be that much poorer in the end.
I think we should set up a conference to study, not just the taxation system but the responsibilities of the two levels of government, and this question of the challenge of foreign competition and the necessity of keeping our place in the export markets should figure very prominently. I have been aware for many years of some of the conflicts which have grown up almost incidentally in the field of taxation. For instance, it is hard to talk to any trucker in western Canada who is not annoyed at the trucking regulations of the province of Ontario. It seems that only certain truckers can get Ontario licences. There are allegations in Alberta that the province of Ontario has set up its trucking regulations in such a way that it is much easier for Ontario truckers to get licences to haul back and forth than it is for Alberta truckers to do so. I have heard allegations made by many trucking firms in Alberta that it is only a chosen few who can get into Ontario at all, whereas the haul from Alberta to Ontario is wide open to competition from Ontario truckers. I am sure members of this committee are aware that interprovincial transportation is a federal responsibility but that the federal government has turned it over to the provincial governments as far as control over trucking is concerned, because administration is easier-the provinces already have responsibility for the licensing and regulation of trucks, and so on. Then there is the question of their responsibility for highway maintenance. These trucks could ruin their roads. In short, there are many good reasons why the provinces should handle this matter. However, I suggest that this conference should take a look at what has happened in the field of interprovincial transportation. I suggest that the question of the amount of money derived from licensing trucks, sales of gasoline, and so on, should be considered again since this is the subject of competition between the provinces and it is something which might better be handled by the federal government which could set up an arrangement based, for instance, on road miles travelled within a province; the federal government could collect the money and remit a due share of it to each of the provinces according to its entitlement.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat, obsessed with the problems of Alberta, mentioned something having to do with education; he made a number of remarks, includ-

ing one about alleged national needs. The hon. member for Jasper-Edson who spoke yesterday might have given the hon. member for Medicine Hat a little lesson on the needs in the field of education. In the province of Alberta the municipalities have to bear a much larger share of the load of education than in any other province. I might say that the efforts of the Social Credit government in Alberta to maintain the pretence that it is a debt free province have perhaps done more than anything else to make it difficult for the province to negotiate with the federal government on legitimate needs of the province, while at the same time it is heaping on the municipal taxpayer the burden of education within that province.
I am not suggesting it is only the province of Alberta that creates or erects artificial barriers because of the kind of political propaganda that a province uses for its own purposes. I am sure that in every province throughout the dominion there is a different method of tax accounting for different purposes. They like to keep their records in a different way and they lay stress to varying degrees on different aspects of governmental problems and responsibilities within their own borders.
It always seems to be the case that as long as there are differences between the provinces on matters of policy it is very hard to say that all Canadians can have an equal opportunity in this country.
With the cost of government being what it is and having in mind the size of the country and the number of governments we have with so few people, I think anyone must concede that one of the reasons the tax load is so heavy is that we are so overgoverned. To me the ideal situation would seem to be that most questions of policy should be decided by the federal government and those that are not should be decided by the provincial governments in conference, so that there would be a standardization of policy in so far as taxation problems are concerned. To that extent the provinces would be more administrative units rather than self-governing entities.
I know this suggestion will be received with many screams in some parts of the country, but I suggest that those who scream the loudest for financial assistance or for financial independence should really be the first to look at their own set ideas, their sacred cows, so to speak, the first to come forward with suggestions as to how there could be more co-operation between the provinces, and as a start could see if a uniform
Federal-Provincial Relations standard of accounting could at least be worked out so that everyone would know where they stood, and everyone who was talking about fiscal policy and taxation would be speaking the same language.
I suggest that there might be a much stricter policy than that laid down for assistance to or interference with private industry within the borders of a province. I suggest that the federal government could play a much stronger role in these negotiations to make sure that there would be uniformity and limits within the provinces. In this way the federal government could keep a very close eye on any policies that would unduly tend to encourage industries to settle in particular provinces, because of what it would do to their export potential. Since the good of Canada must be maintained in order for each province to have a chance to flourish, I suggest this is one field where we must not allow competition to develop to the extent that one province may become healthy in the short term by attracting new industries, only to find that these industries cannot grow to the extent that will really help Canada in the long run.
I do not want to take too long and I have mentioned this subject before, but I do want to emphasize that what is needed is not just short term temporary adjustments in fiscal arrangements such as we are now considering, but rather a very searching look at the rights and responsibilities of the provinces as well as the matter of taxing powers.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to base my comments on the statement the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) made, at the beginning of his speech, when he said everything was going to be the best in the best of all possible worlds and that prosperity seemed to have become the lot of the Canadian people.
I realize that the fact that during the last three months the federal revenue was higher than the expenditures of all departments, should constitute for the minister a sign of prosperity.
But I wonder what will be the reaction of the general public, and especially the 100,000 unemployed in the province of Quebec, if they should happen to read what the minister said about the period of prosperity we are going through?
I wonder also what the numerous people who went bankrupt in the course of the last 12 months will think of the prosperity

Federal-Provincial Relations mentioned a while ago by the Minister of Finance. What will be the reaction of the thousands of farmers whose income is less than $1,200 a year? Will they rejoice with the Minister of Finance at the prosperity Canada has known under the administration we have had for the past two years?
I wonder also what will be the feelings of those who, in the province of Quebec, fell for the policy of grandeur based on the restoring of the province's taxation powers. Indeed, Quebec had been demanding for a couple of years that its taxation powers be restored to her so that she may progress in the field of education and other fields.
I wonder if the people of Quebec who have seen the provincial debt tripled, even quadrupled, will see in the present or future equalization formulas a solution to problems such as the Canadian constitution, taxation and the revenue required by the provincial governments to look after fields coming under their jurisdiction: social security, education, industrial and economic development, development of natural resources, etc.
I wonder what will be the reaction of the small landlords of the province of Quebec who are now overburdened with municipal and school taxes.
I wonder what will be the reaction of the 10,000 farmers who marched on the Quebec parliament, threatening that government to go on a tax strike if the whole municipal, school and provincial taxation structure were not revised.
I wonder if all those people will be, tomorrow, as cheerful as the Minister of Finance was a while ago when he was speaking of our prosperity.
I also wonder whether the Quebec government will find it advisable to appoint an inquiry commission to suggest to both provincial and federal authorities to revamp their taxation structure.
I wonder if they will be satisfied with the small changes which will be made from now until 1967 under this Bill No. C-lll.
Those are some of the questions we had to ask ourselves.
I realize that often when we deal with fiscal matters, threats of separatism-sometimes called excessive-are heard in certain parts of the country.
We are not the only ones, I think, to bear witness on behalf of all Canadians, those from Vancouver as well as those from the province of Quebec. I noted that, yesterday, on the resolution stage. We claim that the present equalization and fiscal system does

not meet, in all fairness, the needs of some provinces. Now, we are not alone, because the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) pointed it out yesterday. In turn, will it be necessary for us to use words that he did not dare utter, but has intimated to say that in British Columbia as well as in Alberta, there is no justice within the fiscal system as it is administered at the present time, in the field of federal and provincial taxation?
I realize that the Minister of Finance might have a certain control over the monetary and financial system in order to regulate the monetary values in the country as much as possible. But what control does he have at the present time?
He has absolutely no control on the issuing of credit. It is undoubtedly for that reason that we see bills come up such as those introduced during this session to set up new chartered banks.
Yet, there are financial institutions such as the "caisses populaires", credit unions and savings banks. But there does not seem to be such a good control over those institutions. That control seems to escape the federal Minister of Finance at the present time.
Therefore, the purpose is probably to strengthen the federal control by the setting up of new chartered banks while remaining within the framework of our present debt system.
During that time, parliament has a good time with federal-provincial conferences, and, for weeks and weeks, people drag on fiscality, taxation, whether at the federal government level, or at the levels of the provincial governments, the municipal councils or the school boards. Whatever the form of taxes levied, direct or indirect, eventually things add up and are reflected in the cost of living. Who suffers the most from this situation? The poor consumer, the humble man, who is indirectly crushed under the burden of taxes, which is being included in the cost of living. The one who suffers most from the situation is the one who is least able to pay.
I wanted to make those remarks because it is already suggested, in certain circles among the public and in the house, that new formulas should be sought to settle the financial and monetary problem, in order to allow, as much as possible, established norms, through standardization in the fields of social security, education, and so forth. But that is always done at the expense of the small fry who, under this system, are always shouldering the heaviest load, so much so that, at a given moment, the majority of the people are in a

state of insecurity for the benefit of the minority. That is what we are opposed to in those fiscal arrangements that settle nothing.
We have been talking about equalization for several years. In 1945, we promised the provinces that they would get back the rights taken away from them at the beginning of the war. We started to hold fiscal conferences and there were meetings between the federal and provincial governments on taxation.
Where do we stand? We are more than ever divided in this country and it will certainly not be fiscal matters which will unite us, but on the contrary, they will divide us even more.
This afternoon the history of a province since confederation was outlined. It would also be useless to outline the history of the ten Canadian provinces because as far as tax matters are concerned, we must face the division and fears of one or the other of the provinces who wishes to grab the better part, while another may pretend that it contributes more than some others.
We are not asking for anything, we do not want to take anything away from the other provinces, but we want the central government to find other ways to solve the problem so that the people can benefit fully from our country's huge resources which are more varied than in any other country in the world. Let us take steps so that the provinces, in their respective fields under the constitution, can exercise their rights as freely as possible. That is what the province of Quebec wants. It has opted out of some joint programs. In the last three or four years, it has withdrawn from several joint programs which would have made it easier for it to develop some natural resources. It gave up those programs and again two days ago we were told that $13 million would be spent on highways, a field which is the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces, to rebuild highway No. 6 in the Gaspe peninsula.
We no longer wish to participate in joint programs because the latter are, in our opinion, an encroachment upon provincial jurisdiction. Nowadays, they are being abandoned for more direct action. Out of some sort of surplus, millions and millions of dollars are being paid under the form of subsidies in fields where the federal government has no business at all.
Consequently, I feel that instead of dividing the country as he is doing at present with respect to taxation, the Minister of Finance should urgently seek other formulas which would set standards under which each prov-
Federal-Provincial Relations ince would get its full share of taxes paid to the federal government. That should be accomplished not through a limitation of the money supply or credit necessary for Canada's expansion but by encouraging better understanding between the provinces and by providing better living conditions for all Canadians.

speechtext:
I wish to rise once again this afternoon to discuss Bill No. C-lll, particularly section 1. I must correct the Minister of Finance with regard to the figures he gave the house this afternoon or ask him to prove that the figures which he obtained are related to the amounts paid by the provinces and redistributed to them by the federal government.
Those figures were supplied by a former Conservative M.P. after he had asked a public servant, in this case Mr. K. Taylor, deputy minister of finance, for them on February 4, 1963. I think that the Minister of Finance, who has just returned to his seat, replied that they had been supplied by the hon. member for Lapointe who, himself, had obtained them from the former M.P. for Sherbrooke, in order to ask the minister to prove that they were genuine or accurate.
If those are not correct figures, then let the Minister of Finance give us more detailed information so that we may know exactly what the situation is. In his reply, the Minister of Finance adhered closely to the letter of the deputy minister, Mr. Taylor, and referred to the four restrictions mentioned by the deputy minister.
So, the minister gave the former member for Sherbrooke the figures concerning amounts paid and, because of those four restrictions, he did not invent those figures but he failed to prove that they were correct. As far as we can rely on the restrictions made by the deputy minister himself, we will accept them. He was rather nebulous and evasive, as he usually is because of his centralizing tendencies.
In quoting those figures the hon. member for Lapointe claimed they were his own. They are not the figures of the Ralliement Credit-iste because they would never have been able to sort out this information-but I ask the minister why, if he wants to give us-

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: To be honest with the hon. member for Lapointe, who is absent this afternoon, I heard him say that he got those figures from Mr. Allard, former Conservative member and now executive assistant
Federal-Provincial Relations to the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer).

My hon. friend who just interrupted, did not listen to the remarks of the hon. member for Lapointe, because I did follow his speech. Besides, he will see in tomorrow's Hansard that it is quite correct. Anyhow, the interruption is of no consequence at all.
The important thing is to get the minister to tell us which figures are correct. As responsible members of the house, we have the right to know what the score really is and it is the duty of the minister to give us the exact figures.
Indeed, a while ago he assured us that he would give some information in the near future. If we go by the record and by the time it takes to give an answer to questions No. 740 and 741 which were put on the order paper by the hon. member for Three Rivers last April 14, we must not expect them soon. If the minister had replied then to those two questions, the debate would probably have been shortened by as much, because we would have known exactly what sums of money had been collected, directly and indirectly, for conditional and unconditional grants to institutions and individuals. We would also have obtained a comparative table of amounts collected by the federal government in each province and their distribution among all provinces.
If the minister assures us that he will provide us with this information, I hope that it will not take another four months, because he is now four months late. I wonder whether we shall have to wait that long, since we are now considering a bill dealing precisely with this particular aspect of federal-provincial relations.
I wonder why the minister does not provide us with this information; since he has very competent and devoted experts working for him, why does he not give us right now the information we have a right to expect and to require from him?
There, Mr. Chairman, is the crucial problem, the source of all the difficulties which arise at federal-provincial conferences. If the minister would give us such information, the situation might be clearer, simpler, and hon. members could then study the matter thoroughly with figures supplied by the minister himself. Mr. Chairman, it is unfortunate that the minister should have almost questioned a little earlier the figures that the deputy minister of finance, Mr. Taylor, gave
[Mr. Drouin.l

a former M.P. in official but not confidential letters.
Mr. Chairman, I hope that the minister will give us those figures soon. I would like him also to tell us when we will get them. Will it be after the bill is passed, or next year, or in the years to come, just like the promises of the Liberal party which seems to make it a point to delay supplying the information that hon. members request.
Mr. Chairman, as we are only discussing the first clause, I want to mention some statements which, without being wrong, nevertheless show that some people do not quite understand the difference there may be between rights conferred to the provinces under the British North America Act and the rights the provinces enjoy with regard to the internal control of their problems. The rights and responsibilities of the provinces in certain priority fields have but too often been confused when speaking of those rights. There obviously are certain responsibilities in some priority areas, but there are also constitutional responsibilities, and those are the ones which Quebec does not want to give up, nor yield.
When speaking of the province of Quebec, I am also conscious of that argument being more and more used by the provinces, because none of them, in the present context of confederation, is ready to yield its constitutional jurisdiction and responsibilities to the central power, as long as the Canadian constitution remains unchanged.
This is precisely the point I wanted to stress, and I do not think it futile nor vague to discuss it and to say that the provinces, though they enjoy certain rights, have to yield them in favour of prior responsibilities which they have in the educational field.
Somebody stated just now that the proof of education being an increasingly important problem in Canada, was that it had been discussed at the provincial premiers' conference in western Canada. But what the hon. member did not say, was that educational problems were not considered under the auspices of the central government, but solely following the impulse given by the provincial premiers who took action in this respect.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to rectify the impression I might have created at the outset, to the effect that the central government must be a strong government. The central government must be strong in its own spheres but on the other hand, it must not be any stronger than the provincial governments in other spheres than its own. I am referring to

education, health, and some fields reserved to them under the B.N.A. Act.
Name those fields.

Mr. Chairman, if my hon. friend for Lotbiniere is in the mood to make jokes about the confederation pact

he knows how-and if he does not know the matters reserved to the provinces under the B.N.A. Act, I advise him to go back to school and then run again as a member of parliament when he has learned certain things.
In the present context of things, the provinces have on many occasions made representations to the central government concerning their own problems. Indeed that matter is of such importance that it was the main item on the agenda of federal-provincial fiscal conferences and I note the lack of consideration of the Liberal members and of the government for that matter.
If the Minister of Finance will be honest toward the citizens he represents, if he is conscious of his responsibilities toward parliament, he will give us, before continuing the discussion on this bill, the figures which he says he has. That might clear up some alleged misunderstanding because of figures quoted by other hon. members. If the minister will give us the assurance that we will get those figures in a not too distant future, we are prepared to accept his explanations. But until then, we wish the minister would carry out the necessary researches and studies in order to provide the house and the members of parliament with the information which could remove these misunderstandings that have been raised by the government itself.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it five o'clock? [Text]

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-49, to amend the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1960, with respect to the quorum of the House of Commons.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it being already about seven minutes after five, and it having been announced we are going to have royal assent at 5.45, this means that this private members' hour has been somewhat truncated. Nevertheless I would hope there would be sufficient agreement to the principle of this bill that

British North America Act we might be able to deal with it even in this short period of time.
The explanatory note to the bill is a very short one. It reads:
The purpose of this bill is to increase the quorum of the House of Commons from 20 to 50 members.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that many members of the house have had the same experience I have had, namely that people outside of the House of Commons are very surprised when they learn what our quorum is. If you ask the average Canadian to guess as to what he thinks is the quorum of the House of Commons where we have 265 members, he will start with 150 or some such large figure. When you tell him it is only 20, he wonders why that quorum is so small. I wondered myself where it originated. I am still searching for the very beginning of this figure, but I have been able to find some interesting information.
When the House of Commons of Canada as we now know it first met in November of 1867, it of course had no rules. It had no Beauchesne. There were certain other people they did not have, and I suppose they were lucky. They had to do something about this matter and accordingly, on the second day of the sitting, November 7, 1867, they did two things. They passed a motion to set up a committee to draft rules for the House of Commons and they passed another motion providing that the rules and regulations of the house of assembly of the late province of Canada should be the rules of this House of Commons until the first committee had made its report.
Well, when you look into the rules of the assembly of the late province of Canada- this is the one that existed between 1841 and 1867-you will find in those rules provision was made for 20 to be the quorum. I remind members, however, that the membership of the house of assembly of the late province of Canada was only 130; 65 from Upper Canada and 65 from Lower Canada. Nevertheless, the figure of 20, which was the quorum for 130 members, was carried over provisionally as the quorum for the House of Commons of 181 members, which was the number we had when we started in 1867. In the meantime, that number of 181 has grown to 265 and our quorum is still the 20 with which we started. It is still the 20 that obtained in 1841 when there were only 130 members in the house of assembly as opposed to our present membership of 265, more than double the membership of 1841.


It is still a matter of curiosity to me as to where the house of assembly, in 1841, got its quorum of 20. I find that that house held its first meeting on June 14, 1841, in the city of Kingston. This was during the period when the parliament of the province of Canada moved about from Kingston, to Montreal, to Quebec city, to Toronto and finally to Ottawa. It met first on June 14, 1841. On June 15 the house passed a motion to the effect that the rules for that house of assembly should be the rules of the old province of Lower Canada. Perhaps some of my hon. friends from Lower Canada, from Quebec, know their history better than I do, but I have not yet been able to find out what the quorum was in Lower Canada and how it ever came to be the quorum. But, Mr. Speaker, in whatever way this figure of 20 was first arrived at, I submit it is completely out of line with the membership of our House of Commons today.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE QUORUM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
We will probably hear from the right hon. gentleman later.
I suggest what we should be concerned about is our own situation, our own feelings about it and what our people think about it. We are all aware of the fact that when people come into the gallery of the house, or hear about our activities either through the press or radio, they are shocked at our attendance which sometimes gets down to 21 or 20, and yet we still carry on.
I also know it is the common thing for us to defend our actions and to defend our public image, but it would be more sensible for us to pay attention to the criticisms which are made of the House of Commons, and if one of those criticisms is that we are not in attendance here as much as we ought to be,

then I think we ought to do something about it. I do not contend that to change the quorum rule will provide lull attendance, but if we did change the quorum rule it would force better attendance because we would not be able to carry on unless we had the number present that is provided for in the rule.
I suggest that in order to make the rule effective and one that would last, we should write it into the constitution, which is where we find it at the present time. It is there is section 48 of the British North America Act, that the presence of at least 20 members is required. So this bill now before us, No. C-49, is proposing an amendment to the British North America Act, changing one word in that section-"twenty" to "fifty"-so that section 48 would then read:
The presence of at least fifty members of the House of Commons shall be necessary to constitute a meeting of the house for the exercise of its powers; and for that purpose the Speaker shall be reckoned as a member.
As I say, this bill if adopted would help to improve our image in the eyes of the Canadian people, and I think that is something we ought to do. I have already said this, but I will say it again, that I do not think we should spend so much time defending our performance as some members do. I think we should respond to some of these criticisms and try to improve our performance, and one of the things we could do is improve our attendance in the House of Commons.
There are a great many aspects and angles to this question, but because of the limited time I shall shorten my remarks and deal with just one main phase of it. One of the main defences that is put up by members of the house for our small attendance-and I should say it is not always small; sometimes the house is very full, but a great deal of the time it gets rather low-is that members have work to do other than their work in the chamber. They have work to do in their offices; and then there are the committees. Of course this is the most abused defence, the fact that there are committees and that members are in those committees instead of being present in the house. Personally I think this excuse is overworked. I do not believe there are any committees meeting right now, yet our attendance is not exactly the 265 which is the membership of the house. Maybe because I have introduced this bill it is a little better than it is sometimes at this hour.
Although this defence about committees is used, as I say I do not think it really stands up. But even so this leads me to just a word 20220-416-1
British North America Act or two I would like to say about the relation between committees and sittings of the house itself. A few references were made earlier to a very interesting experience some of us had last week. I refer to those of us who had the privilege of attending the annual Couchi-ching conference, and I can tell hon. members that the Canadian institute on public affairs will in due course produce a book reporting those proceedings in full. Hon. members will be able to distil for themselves the wisdom that was produced last week. One of the things which was discussed rather fully was the need of making better use of committees in our House of Commons.
I took part in some of these discussions and I made one suggestion at Couchiching last week to which I would like to allude, because I think it has a bearing on this question of our attendance in the house. I suggested that in order to make better use of our committees, in order to bring them to the centre of the stage, to give greater importance to their work, we should reorganize the work of parliament on an annual basis, and I proposed that the session of parliament in a year should be divided into three sections. I suggested that each of these sections might be for about two months. I proposed further that in between these meeetings of the House of Commons as a whole there should be a period of a month here and a month there, when the house does not sit but when the committees do.
I suggested, of course, that attendance in Ottawa when the committees are in session should be just as mandatory upon us, from the standpoint of our pay, as is our attendance in the house. My whole contention was that if we gave the committees the position of being at the centre of the stage, being given the undivided attention of hon. members, we could expect them to do better work.
On some more appropriate occasion I would like to develop that line a little more. Last week was not the first time I suggested it, and I am not the first one to propose it. I wrote an article on this for Queen's Quarterly a decade ago, and it was suggested long before that. I suggest it now for this reason, that if we organize our work in that way, spending part of the year in committees without the house sitting, and spending part of the year back in our constituencies, more than we are now doing, and thus getting the pulse of our people, then the sessions of parliament themselves, say, two months early in the year, two months in the middle of the year and two months toward the end of the year, would

British North America Act command more attendance on our part, and they would be free from meetings of committees that would collide with meetings of parliament. In that way we could expect better attendance and do better work.
These proposals are all tied together and I think it is legitimate for me to mention this one on a simple bill like this, because I do not propose to reform completely the image of parliament by making just one change, namely a change in the quorum. But if this is linked with other kinds of improvements, with planning and organization of the whole work of our parliament, we could do a much better job.
The people of Canada believe that it is our duty to be here, and they have every right to be shocked that our quorum is only 20. The Leader of the Opposition may point to the experience in other countries. We all know the quorum in Westminster is only 40, and they do not pay any great attention to it. Many of us have sat in the gallery at Westminster when attendance was far below 40. In Washington the quorum is the majority of the membership, and they do not pay too much attention to it there either, unless somebody calls attention to the fact that there is not a quorum, and the bells are rung, the representatives or senators are called in, and a roll call made. I do not think very much of that system, any more than does the right hon. gentleman.
In any case, I do not think we can solve our problem by looking at other countries. We have to look at our own situation and I think we are all grateful that the parliamentary system we have is a good one. However I believe it would be much better if we upgraded our committees by some such method as I have suggested, and I believe if we did that it would reduce the number of months we would require to sit in the house, it would produce better attendance on the part of all hon. members, and to that end I put forward this proposal to increase the quorum from 20, which it has been since 1367, even since 1841, to the more reasonable figure of 50.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. Byrne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
It is customary, Mr. Speaker, for me to joust with the hon. member from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on legislation and other matters affecting labour. He of course has studied the rules and forms of parliament to a greater extent than I have; he has had more experience in these matters. But I do feel on equal terms with him when we discuss questions having to do with labour and the


labour movement. I believe even my years give me some advantage in that respect.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Maybe this is part of the parliamentarians' labour code.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
However, I do have some right, I believe, to take part in this debate this afternoon by reason of the many years I have spent in parliament. I have watched its activities for many years; indeed, I believe their number would exceed those of most members of the house. And I have come to the conclusion that there is nothing really wrong with the House of Commons or with its rules. It is, really, the people who make up the House of Commons. It is they who are causing the image of parliament to fail, as the hon. member suggested-if it is failing. It is not because of the rules, but rather because of the people who are here and their disinclination to follow the rules -their disinclination to co-operate with Mr. Speaker so that the house may carry on as it was originally designed to do.
However, I am sure it will be the disposition of those of us who sit on this side of the house to have this matter, which is indeed an important one, brought before the special committee which is presently reviewing the rules of the house. It should be pointed out that in 1867 when the quorum was established there were 181 members, as the hon. member has reminded us. The quorum was set at that time at 20 members. If we were to increase the quorum now to 50 members we would have increased it by 150 per cent, whereas the membership has increased by only 32 per cent.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Did he not hear me point out that the quorum of 20 was actually established in 1841 when the total membership was only 130?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I think I heard the hon. member correctly. But he went further and said it was established by virtue of debating rules which were previously in effect having regard to the membership of the two provinces, which gave a membership of about 120 members. So I was not so far out in the comparison I made.
The hon. member mentioned the committee work and he indicated that the committees did not take up a large part of the time of the members. For this reason he thought the quorum could well stand at 50. I am sure that in 1867 there was much less committee

British North America Act
work, since the affairs of the federal government were less complex and there were fewer subjects for discussion affecting the well-being of Canadians generally. As I have said, I believe it is not the rules as such but our disinclination to follow the rules which causes members to be out of the house. There is little opportunity for them to really take an active part in debates. If members were required to follow the rules strictly, particularly the rule with regard to the reading of speeches; if members could participate in the crossfire of debate such as we have at the opening of the sitting during the question period, there would be an inclination among many members to work longer hours at night and during the lunch hour break to get their office work done so that they could be in the house listening to and taking part in the debates.
However, as hon. members stand up and carefully read long, prepared speeches which might as well, as indeed was suggested the other day, be placed on the record without ever being read, there is an inclination among members generally to go to their offices and do work which is of a constitutional nature having to do with their constituencies. I am sure most members, at least those who did not learn to read under the "See and Do" method, or the "Dick and Jane" method of reading, can read much faster than most people can speak; they can run through Hansard very rapidly and are able to follow in this way what has taken place in this house. So their time is really better occupied in looking after their constituencies, and, of course in committee affairs, than by actually sitting here and listening to speeches being read.
I think that in addition to taking effective steps to discourage the reading of speeches in the house some limitation should be placed on the reading of articles and editorials which appear in newspapers. Of course it is always good publicity for newspapers and editors to have their editorials and other articles read in this chamber. However members of parliament as a general rule read the newspapers voraciously. They are always looking for accounts of what they have said, or what someone else has said, so in all probability they are familiar with what another hon. member proposes to read before he even begins. In addition, of course, it is contrary to the rules to read at length from editorials, bringing before the house the thoughts and opinions of those who were never elected
to represent the people of Canada in this chamber.
Would the hon. member permit a question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Yes.
Does the hon. member not know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) frequently reads from editorials in this house and has done so in this session to justify his course of action?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Yes, I am well aware of that fact. If the hon. member was as familiar with the rules as his confrere, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I think he would realize it is the accepted practice that the Prime Minister and other members of the cabinet may read prepared statements in order that there will be no misunderstanding as to the policy of the government.
I was referring to editorials.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: It is not so important, of course, in the case of a backbencher like myself making statements that may not be related to government policy. But when policy statements are being made by the Prime Minister or other ministers they are reporting on what is actually taking place in their departments, quoting figures and so on. This practice, of course is quite appropriate. But that does not lead toward bringing about participation in a similar way by members on the other side of the house. I have often sat here, as I have done for quite a number of years, when ministers have been making important statements of policy, and the benches on the other side of the house have begun to empty very rapidly indeed.
What about those sitting behind the ministers? Do they listen to the statements?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) has posed the question whether backbenchers behind the ministers listen to statements. I have found that they normally do. They have a very high regard for the frontbenchers. They sit here and listen carefully to what is being said, and I believe even read Hansard the next day because they relish so much what they have heard.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I wonder whether the hon. member would permit another question. Since he is having so much to say about observing the rules we now have, what about the rule of relevancy? The bill before us has

British North America Act to do with the quorum, but the hon. member is wandering all over the lot.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Talk about the Lake Couchi-ching conference.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I have already referred to the rule of relevancy, but if the hon. member will recall the speech he has just made he will remember that he brought up this particular question himself. He said there was a great need for improvement in the rules and certainly observance of the rules. I am saying it is not so much a matter of improving the rules but of observing the existing rules. For instance, a suggestion emanated from that committee for an improvement of standing order 39. The suggestion originated with the subcommittee of which the hon. member is chairman. The new rule provides for lengthening the hours of sitting by half an hour each evening. I find it strange that this should come from the hon. member who, like myself, has always advocated shorter hours.
The net result of this order is to lengthen the sittings. Hon. members arrive at their offices in the morning at eight o'clock, eight thirty or nine o'clock. In the past they had to be here until ten o'clock in the evening, but now they are asked to be here until ten thirty. Certainly the net result has not been to shorten the question period. It has simply given a few extroverts another half hour in Which to get on the pages of Hansard and into the headlines.
The hon. member has also neglected of course to think of the House of Commons staff when lengthening the sittings by half an hour. The queen's printer is also affected because his staff has to prepare Hansard for the next day. The idea behind the rule may have been good but it is difficult to find that this rule has really been useful.
I took some notes while the hon. member was speaking. He did not introduce anything new or anything that will, as I see it, improve the situation in the house. We can talk all we like about the house sitting for two weeks and committees sitting for another two weeks, but when the chips are down members are going to come back into the house and again have their say in order to get it into Hansard and into the headlines. The suggestion that committees sit half the time and the house sit half the time just means we would have to have 18 months sitting in the year rather than 12 months.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The hon. member did not listen very well.
Would the hon. member please tell us what he meant by "when the chips are down" because some of us understand that in a different sense?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Not having the experience and the background of the Leader of the Opposition, and having come from the mines where language is used with somewhat less fluency, I would say that in this case "when the chips are down" means when members are up-
Very good.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
-and want to hear their own voices and get themselves on the record. The hon. member has suggested that more committees should be sitting and more committee work should be done. I hesitate to mention this, but I believe it was the whip of the official opposition who stated in the house the other day-I certainly did not agree with him-that in this session it had been very difficult indeed to get quorums in order that committees might sit. So the committees must already be overworked.
As I said, I am sure it will be the disposition of members on this side of the house to have this matter referred to a committee, but I hope the hon. member will come up with something better than he did in the amendment to standing order 39 (5).

Mr. Speaker, for a few moments I should like to speak on the bill that has been brought before us. I am not in favour of the bill at all for a number of reasons, some of which have already been put forward by the mover of the bill in an attempt to head off, as it were, arguments that might be put forward. However, in my view the arguments that he suggested would come up have not been invalidated, because they are justified.
The hon. member mentioned that in 1841 the quorum of the house was 20 when the total membership was 130 and suggested that on a percentage basis the quorum should therefore be increased at this time. I do not think this is a valid argument at aU. One of the things we have to face, which was mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition, is that in Great Britain there is a quorum of 40 with a membership of over 600. I am sure that the land area represented by those 600 members could be put entirely within my constituency, let alone within a broad country like Canada where members of parliament have to travel 3,000 miles or more to Ottawa, the seat of parliament.

I do not agree that the work of members of parliament is all in the House of Commons or all in committees. I think one not only has an obligation to his own constituency but should travel throughout the country to find out at first hand exactly what people are thinking and saying and what their problems are, so that in our position as members we will have a background of information to call upon in adjudicating on those matters that are presented to us.
Further than that, if we increase to 50 the number of members to constitute a quorum we must remember there are those who are the faithful sitters and those who are unfaithful in regard to their attendance in the house. Therefore those who are available will be penalized that much more and their work will lag because of the attitude they have towards this chamber. That will again cause unnecessary hardship.
With regard to the argument about committees and the other work a member of parliament has, one of the members from the hon. member's own party this afternoon had to get an additional secretary to do a lot of the extra work which he has as a member of parliament. These arguments are valid and we cannot confine our work. As a matter of fact, one of the reasons we have a Hansard, which I sincerely believe is part of this institution, is so that members who cannot sit each day in the house can refer to Hansard and get the gleanings of what has been said in order that they can judge the better what is to be their position with regard to any issue.
The suggestion that committees sit for a certain period and that then parliament would sit would require close scrutiny. My observations in this House of Commons, although I have not been here nearly as long as the hon. member, and I am sure I have not been on my feet as often as he, lead me to think that we would have to look very carefully into the proposition of dividing parliament into sections. I think we as members of parliament must work closely with the committees of the house because their activities are interrelated with those of the house. By having a committee sit at the same time as the house we have the advantage of being up to date on matters before parliament.
I might mention that we have been waiting for some time now for a report from the standing committee on privileges and elections to come down, and I have heard grumblings and rumblings about the fact that this report has not yet been brought down. If a
British North America Act standing committee deals with a certain matter-let us take as an example the Columbia river treaty-and the house does not sit for two or three months after the matter has been disposed of by the committee, I do not think the matter should be put into a box or a pigeonhole, because the business of the House of Commons and its committees, is as I say, very much interrelated.
With regard to the question of setting up an agenda for our committees and how the committees will operate, I think there is a snag in this regard. I do not think we are prepared to meet our obligations in connection with committees without doing a great deal of work. Will this question of the agenda be purely a matter for the government?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: It will be by reference from the house.

So the hon. member says. But we are in a changing world, and at times emergencies arise and the house should be reconvened if it is not in session. Personally, I do not accept the proposition, although my mind is not closed at all and the hon. member may yet convince me.
But getting back to the question of the quorum and the argument about what the people in the country think about the number of members sitting at any time in the House of Commons, if the quorum were raised to 50 it would not change people's attitudes. There are those in the gallery at the moment who are listening to one speaker speaking his mind. There are so many speakers in an afternoon, and that is parliament, regardless of whether 25 members or 50 are in the house. I do not think it will make any difference to the impression which the public has of parliament.
I think we must look at the problem much more closely, in spite of what I have heard this afternoon. Frankly, at the moment I am not in favour of increasing the quorum to 50. There may be an argument for bringing it up to 25 or even 30, but certainly not 50. As I say, long distances are involved. Members are called upon to travel across Canada in order to carry on in full their parliamentary duties; and let no one make any mistake that that is not part of the duties of a member of parliament serving his constituency. Those members whose constituencies are in close proximity to this house in Ottawa may find it convenient to slip off on a Friday and come back late Monday afternoon or Tuesday morning, and possibly this is the gripe which the hon. member has in

British North America Act mind; but the faithful attenders in the house will be here and they are the ones who are here steadily. Those people who are in the habit of taking off on week ends will still take off on week ends, regardless, and the situation will not improve at all.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minisier of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house believe that the question of the number of members necessary to form a quorum in the house is worthy of further consideration. Therefore I move, seconded by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer):
That Bill No. C-49 be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the special committee on procedure and organization.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I move the adjournment of the debate.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Closure.
